title: Build every ad concept from one persona, one angle, one offer
hypothesis: If every new ad changes at least one of persona, angle, or offer, then it reaches genuinely new buyers, because format alone adds only weak reach.

signal.check: List the last 10 live ads. If most differ only in image, color, or actor and not in who they target or what they claim, this idea is live.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no source measures this directly

risk.note: A stricter concept definition can slow batch output if the team has few real concept ideas ready.

prerequisites: A written list of the brand's personas, angles, and offers
steps: List the brand's current personas, angles, and offers on one page.
For every planned ad, mark which of persona, angle, or offer it changes.
Relabel any ad that changes only design or format as a variant, not a new concept.
Send true concept changes to the concept board before any design work starts.

test.method: Run one batch built strictly on this rule next to a normal batch and compare which produces more winners.
test.read_point: After 2 to 3 full test packs, about 3 to 4 weeks

title: Do not count a color, pose, or model swap as a new ad test
hypothesis: If we only launch variants that change angle, offer, persona, or format, then test spend stops going to changes too small to measure or to beat delivery grouping.

signal.check: Check the last batch's variant list. If most 'new ads' differ only in background, pose, or color, this idea is live.

expected_effect.size: a minor variant's effect is estimated at 1% to 2%, usually too small to measure

risk.note: Being too strict about what counts as a test can slow volume if the team has no real concept ideas ready.

prerequisites: A written definition of what counts as a new concept
steps: Before launch, write what changed in the concept versus the last ad.
If only design, color, pose, or background changed, label it a variant, not a test.
Reserve test-pack slots for changes big enough to move angle, offer, persona, or format.
Track how many 'tests' each month were actually design tweaks.

test.method: Tag each launch as a real test or a design variant for one month and compare read quality between the two groups.
test.read_point: End of one month of tagged launches

title: Write the ad's concept before opening a design tool or booking a shoot
hypothesis: If the team writes what the ad must say before building it, then less budget goes into assets built around the wrong idea.

signal.check: Ask about the last 3 briefs whether the concept was written before or after the shoot or design file was opened.

expected_effect.size: about 80% of round time should go to research and concepting before building

risk.note: Adding a planning step can feel slow to a team used to building fast, so keep it short.

steps: Before any shoot or design file, write the concept row: persona, angle, offer, stage.
Answer what this ad must say about this product, price, and offer.
Only after that, decide the format and open the design tool or book the shoot.

test.method: Compare revision count and rework cost on briefed-first assets against assets built ad hoc.

title: Write the angle as one sentence for one persona before scripting
hypothesis: If the angle is one sentence naming the persona, the problem, and the proof, then every line in the ad can be checked against it, so cold ads stop reading like an infomercial.

signal.check: Read the last cold ad's script or copy. If it lists many reasons to buy instead of building one argument, this idea is live.

risk.note: A single strong angle can undersell a product with many real selling points, so plan a separate ad per major reason.

prerequisites: Research notes on the persona's language and problem
steps: Write the angle as: who, the product, why it solves their problem, the proof.
Check every line of the draft ad against that one sentence.
Cut lines that support a different reason to buy; save them as a separate angle.

test.method: Have someone outside the team read the ad and say the angle back in one sentence.
test.read_point: Before launch, then against the account's hook rate after day 7

title: Build the angle from proof and pain components, not a feature list
hypothesis: If the angle is built from components such as problem agitation, contrarian truth, proof, and transformation instead of a feature list, then the ad reads as an argument, not a spec sheet.

signal.check: Read the ad's copy blocks. If it is mostly features and specs with no problem or proof block, this idea is live.

risk.note: Adding every component makes an ad too long; pick the components the stage and persona need.

prerequisites: Angle sentence (R4)
steps: List the available components: problem agitation, contrarian truth, social proof, domain authority, curiosity gap, comparison, transformation.
Pick 2 to 4 components that fit the persona's awareness stage.
Match proof choices to the persona's age and profile.
Write the script or copy using only those blocks.

test.method: Compare a components-built ad against a features-led ad on the same offer.

title: Split the mechanism into why the problem happens and why the fix works
hypothesis: If the script explains both why the viewer has the problem and why the product fixes it, then the claim reads as reasoned, not asserted, and trust rises.

signal.check: Read the script or copy. If it states a benefit with no cause given for the problem or the fix, this idea is live.

risk.note: A mechanism explanation that is too technical can lose cold viewers; keep it simple and new.

prerequisites: Real product facts and the reason it works
steps: Write why the viewer has the problem in one line.
Write why this product fixes it in one line.
Keep both simple, intuitive, and specific to the product, not generic.
Tie the mechanism to the founder story, ingredient, material, or craft where true.

test.method: A/B a script with the mechanism spelled out against one that only asserts the benefit.

title: When a concept stops converting, retest angle, then offer, then persona, then format
hypothesis: If a failing concept is retested in the order angle, offer, persona, format, then the team fixes the most likely cause first instead of reshooting in a random order.

signal.check: A concept that used to convert is now flat or declining, and the next step has not been decided.

risk.note: This order is one agency's opinion; a brand's own past tests may show a different order works better.

prerequisites: Past buyers already proven for this persona
steps: Confirm past buyers exist for this persona, which rules out persona as the first suspect.
Test a new angle on the same offer and persona first.
If the angle test fails, test a new offer next.
Only after that, test a new persona, then a new format.

test.method: Follow this order on the next fatigued concept and log which step revived it.

title: Treat the offer as a concept lever, not a discount
hypothesis: If the offer is varied as a bundle, tiered quantity, or subscription instead of a straight discount, then the store can raise AOV without eating margin on every sale.
does_not_apply_when: a brand that cannot bundle or tier its product

signal.check: Check whether the only offer variable tested in the last quarter was a percent-off discount.

expected_effect.size: for low unit price products, 3, 5, or 6 packs to reach roughly $25 to $30 AOV

risk.note: A bundle sized wrong can hurt margin as much as a discount; check contribution margin before launch.

prerequisites: Margin room to build bundles (see 03-OFF)
steps: List possible offer framings: bundle, gift with purchase, tiered quantity discount, subscription, packaging change.
Check contribution margin at each framing.
Build a concept row per offer framing, not just per discount depth.
For a low unit price product, test a 3, 5, or 6 pack version.

test.method: Run a bundled-offer ad against the standard discount ad on the same concept.

title: Name the functional or emotional problem the product solves before writing an ad
hypothesis: If the team names the specific problem, functional or emotional, that the product solves, then the ad has a reason to agitate instead of just describing the product.

signal.check: Ask the team what problem the product solves. If the answer is only a feature or category name, this idea is live.

risk.note: Forcing a heavy problem onto a light, fun product can feel dishonest; match the tone to the category.

steps: Write the problem the product solves in plain words.
Decide if it is functional (does a job) or emotional (feel cool, feel part of something).
For light or impulse products, lean on fast attention and humor instead of heavy agitation.
For private or sensitive problems, route the tone toward curiosity and a quiz or education page.

test.method: Write two versions, problem-led and product-led, and compare hook rate.

title: Write cold hooks for self-recognition, not for wide appeal
hypothesis: If a cold hook is written so only the target buyer says this is my exact problem, then it filters out the wrong viewers and holds the right ones, even though it will fail with everyone else.

signal.check: The team is optimizing a hook to appeal to a broad audience instead of one ICP.

risk.note: An ad built for one ICP is expected to fail with others; do not read that as a bad ad.

prerequisites: A sharp persona (R11)
steps: Write the hook so it names the exact problem one persona has.
Accept that people outside that persona will scroll past.
Judge the hook by whether the target persona stops, not by overall appeal.

test.method: Compare a self-recognition hook against a broad-appeal hook on the same body.

title: Slow the agitation for luxury, considered, or gift products
hypothesis: If a luxury, considered-purchase, or gifting brand slows the agitation and weights proof toward craft, material, and provenance, then the ad avoids the mismatch of a direct-response health template on a high-ticket product.
does_not_apply_when: a low-ticket or impulse product

signal.check: Check whether the brand's current ad templates were copied from a supplement or DR health playbook.

risk.note: Untested for fashion, jewelry, or high-ticket goods per the source; treat as a hypothesis to verify with the brand's own data.

prerequisites: Real product photos and provenance facts
steps: Slow the agitation pace compared to a DR health template.
Weight proof toward craft, material, and provenance over price objections.
Treat a gift occasion as an offer variable, not just a seasonal banner.
Test the slower-paced version against the brand's current fast-paced template.

test.method: Run a slow-agitation, craft-led ad against the brand's current template on the same audience.

title: Build personas from customer language, not age or gender labels
hypothesis: If personas are built from what customers say in reviews, tickets, and surveys instead of demographic labels, then the resulting script, talent, and proof choices become specific enough to convert.
does_not_apply_when: a brand doing a broad unaware campaign at very large scale, which the source says needs a different skill level

signal.check: Check the persona document. If personas read as 'women 25 to 45' or 'busy professional' with no problem language, this idea is live.

risk.note: None; this only improves how personas are described.

prerequisites: Review, ticket, and survey exports
steps: Pull raw quotes from reviews, tickets, and post-purchase surveys.
Write each persona as outcome times demographic times facet, for example a state, event, or condition.
Drop any persona defined only by age or gender with no stated problem.
Check that each persona could tell a writer the script, the talent, and the proof needed.

test.method: Compare an ad built on a language-based persona against one built on a demographic label.

title: Build the persona list by hand first, then expand it with AI in two rounds
hypothesis: If the team writes 20 to 40 personas by hand before asking an AI tool for more, then the AI expansion adds real variety instead of the generic answer everyone gets from 3 personas and a URL.

signal.check: Check whether the current persona list came only from an AI prompt with little manual input.

expected_effect.size: 20 to 40 by hand, then roughly doubled by AI in two expansion rounds

risk.note: Skipping the manual step and going straight to AI gives generic archetypes.

prerequisites: P1 research document
steps: Spend about 20 minutes listing who buys and what problem the product solves for each.
List 2 to 4 core personas, then drill into problem variants for each.
Write each as outcome times demographic times facet.
Aim for 20 to 40 personas by hand.
Give the full list plus business and customer context to an AI tool and ask for 20 to 30 more.
Keep the 4 to 5 best, feed them back, and ask for 10 to 20 more.
Flag any persona defined by a personal attribute for a policy check.

test.method: Compare ad performance from a hand-plus-AI persona list against a pure-AI list.

title: Run a research sprint across reviews, tickets, and comments before any brief
hypothesis: If the team blocks time to read raw customer language before writing any brief, then angles and objections come from real repeated statements instead of guesses.
does_not_apply_when: a brand with no review, ticket, or survey history yet

signal.check: Check whether the last concept board was built without reading reviews, tickets, or ad comments first.

expected_effect.size: block 3 to 4 days for a new niche, about 80% of round time on research and concepting

risk.note: An AI summary with no raw quotes read by a human is not a substitute for this step.

prerequisites: Access to review, ticket, and survey exports
steps: Block time in proportion to how unfamiliar the niche is.
Read reviews, tickets, survey answers, ad comments, and competitor reviews, and paste raw quotes into one document.
Sort every statement into what they want, what stops them, what they already tried.
Cluster by repetition and count occurrences per cluster.
Write each cluster as a one-sentence angle, keeping the customer's wording.
Mark the awareness stage, proof available, and any compliance flag next to each angle.

test.method: Check every angle traces to at least 2 quotes; audit a sample of angles against the raw document.
test.read_point: At the end of the research sprint

title: Turn every repeated want, blocker, and past attempt into an ad idea
hypothesis: If research is sorted into what customers want, what stops them, and what they already tried, then each strong repeated statement becomes a usable ad idea instead of being lost in a document.

signal.check: The research document has raw quotes but no list of derived angles or objections.

risk.note: A one-off mention is not an angle; only repeated use cases count.

prerequisites: Research sprint document (R13)
steps: Sort every quote into three buckets: what they want, what stops them, what they already tried.
Flag repeated use cases, such as the same product used in several different settings, as separate angles.
Drop one-off mentions from the angle list.
Use the 'what they already tried' bucket to build objection-handling ads.

test.method: Count how many angles in the next board trace to a repeated customer statement.

title: Write hooks and copy in the customer's own in-group words
hypothesis: If hooks use the niche terms and phrasing customers already use, then the ad reads as written by an insider instead of a generic brand voice.

signal.check: Compare the ad's wording to the exact phrases customers use in reviews and comments; if they do not match, this idea is live.

risk.note: An AI tool alone will not reliably produce niche humor or in-group jokes.

prerequisites: Research sprint document (R13)
steps: Pull the exact niche terms and phrases from reviews and comments.
Write hooks and headlines using that language, not a generic paraphrase.
Have a real member of the niche or an experienced writer check the wording before launch.

test.method: Compare a niche-language hook against a generic-wording hook on the same body.

title: Keep benefit pillars broad enough to cover the real market
hypothesis: If brand-level benefit pillars stay broad enough to apply without the core activity or superuser trait, then the addressable market does not shrink to a niche too small to scale.
does_not_apply_when: a brand deliberately targeting a narrow niche as its whole strategy

signal.check: Check the brand's core pillars. If they require a specific activity or trait the majority of buyers do not have, this idea is live.

risk.note: A single ad can still be specific to one persona; it is the brand-level pillars that must stay broad.

steps: List the brand's core benefit pillars.
Check each against whether it requires a specific activity, identity, or trait to matter.
Rewrite pillars that only fit a narrow superuser group to be usable by the wider real market.
Keep individual ads specific to one persona while the pillar set stays broad.

test.method: Compare CPA on ads built from broad pillars against ads built from a narrow niche pillar.

title: Open new personas or use-case facets once the main persona plateaus
hypothesis: If the team lists other real problems the same product solves for a different person, then spend can grow past the main persona's ceiling without inventing benefits the product does not have.
does_not_apply_when: a brand still growing on its main persona with no plateau

signal.check: Check frequency and CPA trend on the main persona's campaigns. Rising frequency or CPA with flat spend growth is the plateau signal.

risk.note: Only claim benefits the product genuinely has; do not invent a new use case.

prerequisites: Frequency, reach, and CPA trend data for the main persona
steps: Pull frequency and CPA trend for the main persona over the last 30 to 60 days.
List other real problems the same product solves for a different person or use case.
Write each as a new persona with its own facet, not a copy of the main one.
Build a small test pack around the strongest new facet.

test.method: Launch a pack for the new facet and compare its CPA against the plateaued main persona.

title: Pull ad ideas from several sources, not just competitors or the team's own head
hypothesis: If the idea pipeline draws from swipes, templates, organic research, the segment-format matrix, and the brand's own account patterns, then the batch avoids the low hit rate of copying only competitors or reusing only proven templates.

signal.check: Check where the last batch's ideas came from. If all of them trace to competitor swipes or the team's own head, this idea is live.

risk.note: Under the competitor-copying rule, only layout, structure, and mood may be borrowed, never text, logos, or claims.

prerequisites: Ad Library access; the brand's own tagged ad history
steps: List idea sources: swipes, templates, organic research, the segment-format matrix, internal account patterns, new styles, and higher-risk gambles.
Pull at least one idea from 3 or more of these sources for the next batch.
When studying competitors, focus on brands 1 to 2 steps above the brand, not giants or too-small brands.
Rewrite any borrowed idea in the brand's own words with its own assets.

test.method: Tag each idea's source in the batch and compare hit rate by source over a quarter.

title: Build a VSL only when the product needs real education to convert
hypothesis: If a VSL is built only for a complicated product, a low-trust category, a new ingredient, or a cold conversion rate capped by misunderstanding, then production time is not spent on a format the product does not need.
does_not_apply_when: a simple, well-understood product with no cold-conversion cap

signal.check: Check whether cold conversion is capped and buyers seem not to understand the product, or whether a VSL is being copied just because it worked for another brand.

risk.note: Do not build a VSL just because it worked for a supplement brand; check the product actually needs the education.

steps: Ask whether the product is complicated, in a low-trust category, or uses a new ingredient or mechanism.
Check whether cold conversion is capped because buyers do not understand the product.
If none of these apply, do not build a VSL; use a shorter format instead.
If one applies, proceed to script the VSL.

test.method: Compare cold conversion between a VSL and a shorter video on the same concept before committing further production.

title: Script the VSL in 7 parts from hook to CTA
hypothesis: If a VSL follows hook, problem in the customer's words, mechanism, objection handling, bridge to product, proof, risk reversal, then CTA, then it covers what a long-form education-led ad needs to actually close a sale.

signal.check: Check whether the current VSL script is missing any of the 7 parts, especially objection handling or risk reversal.

risk.note: The order can flex; the parts themselves should still all appear.

prerequisites: Objection list from customer research
steps: Write the hook naming who has the problem, never a brand story.
State the problem in the customer's own words without naming the product.
Explain the mechanism, giving each ingredient or feature its why.
Handle objections from customer data.
Bridge to the product, then stack proof and a risk reversal.
Close with a clear CTA.

test.method: Compare conversion between a full 7-part script and the current script missing parts.

title: Start VSL length short and cut down further, not the reverse
hypothesis: If a VSL master is built around 3 to 4 minutes and then cut into shorter 2-to-3-minute and 45-second versions, then the team avoids wasting a 60-minute script that nobody watches.

signal.check: Check whether the team is planning a very long VSL script before any shorter version exists.

expected_effect.size: VSLs run about 90 seconds to 20 minutes; 3 to 4 minutes is normal, cut down to 2 to 3 minutes and 45 seconds

risk.note: None; this is a production sequencing choice.

steps: Write the master script at about 3 to 4 minutes.
Cut a 2-to-3-minute version from the same master.
Cut a 45-second version as a further variant.
Test all three lengths rather than only launching the longest one.

test.method: Compare hold rate and CPA across the 3 lengths.

title: Judge VSL economics on repeat purchase, and pace for an older audience
hypothesis: If a VSL's return is judged including repeat purchase, not just first-order ROAS, then a brand with real repeat rate can justify a VSL that would look unprofitable on first order alone.
does_not_apply_when: a one-off or gift purchase brand with low repeat rate

signal.check: Check whether VSL economics are judged only on first-order ROAS with no repeat-purchase data included.

expected_effect.size: one account example: about 2.5 to 3x new-customer ROAS with most profit from repeat purchase

risk.note: A product with genuinely low repeat purchase may not survive judging on first-order ROAS alone at this format's cost.

prerequisites: Repeat rate and lifetime value data
steps: Pull repeat rate and 12-month value alongside first-order ROAS for VSL traffic.
Recompute the VSL's real return including repeat purchase.
For an older-skewing audience, keep on-screen text large and pacing quick.

test.method: Compare first-order ROAS against a repeat-purchase-adjusted ROAS for the same VSL cohort.

title: Keep a clear CTA on the first VSL rather than testing a no-CTA version
hypothesis: If the first VSL a brand runs keeps a clear CTA and simple retargeting, then it avoids the added complexity of a no-CTA, pure-awareness VSL before the format has proven itself.

signal.check: Check whether the team is planning a no-CTA VSL as its first VSL test.

risk.note: A no-CTA VSL is a valid later test once the format is proven; just not as the first one.

steps: Keep a clear CTA on the asset for the first VSL.
Keep the retargeting plan simple rather than building a complex view-percentage audience strategy.
Save a no-CTA, pure-awareness VSL test for after the format has proven itself.

test.method: Launch the first VSL with a CTA and measure conversion before testing a no-CTA version later.

title: Pair advertorial and listicle funnels with a real educational page or long copy
hypothesis: If an advertorial or listicle static is paired with a genuine educational page or heavy education in the primary text, then the funnel actually teaches instead of just baiting a click with no follow-through.

signal.check: Check whether a curiosity or advertorial-style static sends clicks to a page with no real education, such as a bare PDP.

risk.note: Any brand-owned educational page must present itself as the brand's own content, never as an independent review site, and rivals must never be shown with fake comparisons.

prerequisites: A real educational page, ranking page, or quiz to route to
steps: Build or confirm a genuine educational page, listicle, or quiz for the funnel.
Make sure the page discloses it belongs to the brand.
Match the static's curiosity or advertorial style to that page, not a bare PDP.

test.method: Compare downstream conversion between the advertorial-to-education-page funnel and a direct-to-PDP version.

title: Build separate creative for the first box, renewal, and win-back on subscription
hypothesis: If a subscription brand builds distinct creative for the first box, the renewal, and a win-back message instead of one generic subscription ad, then each stage of the subscriber lifecycle gets a message that fits it.
does_not_apply_when: a one-off purchase brand

signal.check: Check whether the same subscription ad is currently used for new sign-ups, renewals, and win-backs alike.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source; verify with brand data

risk.note: This folder's sources cover subscription only as an offer type; treat this as an untested hypothesis to verify.

prerequisites: Subscription lifecycle stages and churn data
steps: Write a first-box ad focused on what to expect and why to start.
Write a renewal ad focused on continued value and satisfaction.
Write a win-back ad addressing why a lapsed subscriber left.
Route each to the audience segment matching its lifecycle stage.

test.method: Compare churn and reactivation rate between lifecycle-specific creative and the current generic ad.

title: Run a portfolio of many live concepts, never just 1 to 3 hero ads
hypothesis: If the account keeps many live, profitable concepts instead of concentrating spend in 1 to 3 hero ads, then a single ad fatiguing does not sink the account's growth.

signal.check: Check the spend share of the top 1 to 3 ads this month. If they hold most of the account's spend with nothing new behind them, this idea is live.

expected_effect.size: one case: 3 creatives held $1M and needed fixing 6 to 8 months earlier than the brand did

risk.note: Treat creative production as a revenue driver, not a cost to cut, even during a strong month.

prerequisites: Spend share by ad by month
steps: Check the top 1 to 3 ads' spend share monthly.
If they hold most of the account's spend, start production 6 to 8 months before a likely decline, not after.
Run every concept that is profitable at its own spend level, not just the single best ROAS.
Fund production as a revenue driver in the budget, not as a line item to cut first.

test.method: Track new-customer revenue and top-3 spend share monthly as the portfolio broadens.

title: Set the store's own quality bar from past winners before counting any ad toward volume
hypothesis: If a brand defines its own 7-out-of-10 ad from past winners and only counts ads above that bar toward the monthly volume target, then volume growth does not mistrain the pixel with low-quality output.

signal.check: Check whether the volume target counts every launched ad, with no quality bar applied before it counts.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 accounts launching 2,000+ ads a month were unprofitable

risk.note: Only winners should count; total ad count alone means nothing.

prerequisites: A sample of the brand's own past winning ads
steps: Review the brand's own best-performing past ads.
Define what a 7-out-of-10 ad looks like for this brand specifically.
Score every new ad against that bar before it counts toward the monthly target.
If hit rate falls as volume rises, cut volume and raise the bar.

test.method: Track hit rate against volume monthly to see if quality is diluting.

title: Size monthly ad volume from the account's own hit rate and economics
hypothesis: If monthly ad volume is computed from the account's own mean spend per ad, expected revenue per ad, and hit rate, then production targets match the account's real capacity instead of a flat rule of thumb.
does_not_apply_when: a brand with no ad history yet, which should use the $1,000-per-ad fallback

signal.check: Check whether the current monthly ad count target comes from a flat rule with no reference to the account's own hit rate or spend per ad.

expected_effect.size: fallback with no history: 1 new ad per $1,000 of monthly spend; hit rate is typically 5% to 15%

risk.note: Do the arithmetic in code with the brand's real data, not by hand from memory.

prerequisites: 12 months of ads launched, spend, revenue per ad, winners, and churn
steps: Pull 12 months of ads launched, spend, new customer revenue, winners, and churned winners.
Compute mean spend per ad, expected revenue per ad, hit rate, and churn.
Compute ads needed by revenue target divided by expected revenue per ad, and by churned winners divided by hit rate.
Use the $1,000-per-ad fallback only where no history exists.

test.method: Compare the computed volume target against the account's actual results over the next quarter.

title: Set production budget by spend tier, then replace it with real per-ad profit
hypothesis: If production budget is set by the account's spend tier as a starting point, then replaced with real per-ad gross-profit data once it exists, then a brand with no history still gets a sensible starting budget.
does_not_apply_when: a brand that already has reliable per-ad production cost and profit data

signal.check: Check whether production budget is set with no reference to spend tier or to real per-ad economics.

expected_effect.size: roughly 25% of media at $30K to $100K monthly spend, falling toward about 10% above $100K

risk.note: These are one agency's tier figures in AUD; use them only until the brand's own per-ad data exists.

steps: Identify the brand's current monthly spend tier.
Set an initial production budget share using the tier default.
Track per-ad production cost and revenue as data accumulates.
Replace the tier default with the brand's own gross-profit-per-ad formula once enough data exists.

test.method: Compare gross profit per ad under the tier default budget against a recalculated budget from real data.
test.read_point: After 3 months of tagged production cost data

title: Split production effort: mostly replication and iteration, always some net-new
hypothesis: If production effort splits roughly 50% to 60% replication, 20% to 30% iteration, and 20% to 30% net-new, never zero net-new, then the batch builds on what works while still guarding against total portfolio fatigue.

signal.check: Check whether the current production plan has 0% net-new concepts, only variants of existing winners.

expected_effect.size: replication 50% to 60%, iteration 20% to 30%, net new 20% to 30%

risk.note: Replication alone is the pattern the sources call 'the old way', which ends with all spend in a few fatiguing creatives.

steps: Tag each planned asset in the next batch as replication, iteration, or net-new.
Check the split against the 50-60 / 20-30 / 20-30 targets.
Add net-new concepts from the gap matrix if that share is at or near zero.

test.method: Track hit rate by effort category over a quarter.

title: Pace how hard a winner is pushed by inventory and cash, not ROAS alone
hypothesis: If a winner is squeezed hard when stock needs clearing and allowed to breathe at lower spend when stock or cash is tight, then scaling decisions stop causing stockouts or piled-up cash in stock.
does_not_apply_when: a brand with no inventory constraint, such as a pure dropship or on-demand model

signal.check: Check whether a winning ad is being scaled with no reference to current stock level or cash conversion cycle.

risk.note: An agency squeezing a winner for a case study can cause stockouts and shorten the account's useful life.

prerequisites: Stock by SKU and cash conversion cycle data
steps: Pull days of stock and cash conversion cycle for the SKU behind the winning ad.
If stock needs clearing, raise budget to squeeze the winner faster.
If stock or cash is tight, hold spend lower for longer instead of a short aggressive push.
Build creative for slow-moving stock even at lower efficiency where needed.

test.method: Track stockout days and cash conversion cycle as scaling pace changes.

title: Build a bundle or clearance creative type made to move slow-moving stock
hypothesis: If a dedicated bundle or clearance creative type is built specifically to move slow-moving SKUs, then inventory pacing and offer construction connect into one deliberate creative lane instead of staying separate ideas.
does_not_apply_when: a hero-SKU store with no slow-moving inventory problem

signal.check: Check whether any SKU has high days of stock with no dedicated ad built to move it.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source; verify with brand data

risk.note: Check margin room before bundling; a badly sized bundle can hurt margin as much as a discount.

prerequisites: Days of stock by SKU
steps: Identify SKUs with high days of stock.
Build a bundle or clearance offer sized to move that SKU, checked against margin.
Write a dedicated ad for it, tagged separately from standard concept-board rows.
Track days of stock for that SKU after launch.

test.method: Compare days of stock for the flagged SKU before and after the clearance creative launches.

title: Run creative as a monthly pipeline where each test result writes the next brief
hypothesis: If material is collected all month and each test's result directly shapes the next brief, a winning angle gets more creatives, a losing format gets dropped, then the creative process stops producing disconnected one-off ads.

signal.check: Check whether last month's briefs referenced the results of the previous batch, or were written independently of them.

risk.note: Expect most individual ads to fail even inside a good pipeline; the pipeline's job is to learn fast, not to make every ad win.

prerequisites: A weekly or monthly review cadence
steps: Collect research material and comments continuously through the month.
Script in bulk rather than one script at a time.
Feed each test's result into the next brief: expand a winning angle, drop a losing format, turn a competitor weakness into an objection ad.
Review the account, competitors, and the market on a set weekly or monthly cadence.

test.method: Check whether each new brief cites a specific result from the prior batch.

title: Track the current live library's format and stage coverage against the 3.10 tier defaults
hypothesis: If the number of active concepts, creators, and monthly new creatives is checked against the spend-tier defaults, then the team notices when production has fallen behind the account's own growth stage.

signal.check: Count current active concepts and monthly new creatives, and compare against the tier defaults for this spend level.

expected_effect.size: 3 active concepts under $30K per month, 5 to 6 at $30K to $100K, 8 to 10 above $100K

risk.note: These are one agency's tier defaults; treat as a starting checkpoint, not a hard rule.

steps: Determine the account's current monthly spend tier.
Count active concepts and monthly new creatives currently in production.
Compare against the tier default and flag a gap for the next planning cycle.

test.method: Recheck this count monthly as spend changes tier.

title: Give every test a written hypothesis before it launches
hypothesis: If every test states the concept, the one variable under test, expected spend, conversions, and return before launch, then the team can compare expected against actual instead of reading results with no baseline.

signal.check: Check whether the last test pack launched with no written hypothesis or expected numbers.

risk.note: Only run tests that are measurable, worth the spend, and would change what the team makes next.

steps: Name the concept and the one variable under test.
Write expected spend, expected conversions, and expected return before launch.
Compare actual results against these expectations after the read.
Record whether the hypothesis was confirmed, in the DNA sheet.

test.method: Audit the next 5 test packs for a written hypothesis before launch.

title: Keep one persona-and-angle pair per ad set so results can be read cleanly
hypothesis: If each ad set carries exactly one persona-and-angle pair, then the store can see which segment and message actually drives purchases instead of reading a mixed-concept ad set's spend as one blur.
does_not_apply_when: a brand deliberately running a separate test of one ad set for all stages

signal.check: Check whether a current ad set mixes more than one persona or angle.

risk.note: This is a deployment-facing structure rule; the creative agent writes it into the test plan for 24-DEP to execute.

steps: Check each planned ad set for a single persona-and-angle pair.
Split any mixed ad set into separate ad sets by concept.
Write this structure into the test plan handed to deployment.

test.method: Compare read clarity between a single-concept ad set and a mixed one over one batch.

title: Size every pack to 4 to 8 ads and plan 10 or more ads per concept
hypothesis: If a pack holds 4 to 8 ads, at least 3, and a concept gets 10 or more ads across packs, then the daily budget can actually take the pack to a real read instead of spreading spend too thin to learn anything.

signal.check: Check whether the last pack held more ads than the daily budget could fund to a read, or fewer than 3.

expected_effect.size: 4 to 8 ads per pack, minimum 3, 10 or more ads per concept across packs

risk.note: Never go below 4 ads per pack to fit a tighter budget; cut the number of packs instead.

prerequisites: Daily budget per pack and target CPA
steps: Check the daily budget against target CPA to see how many ads it can fund to a read.
Size the pack to 4 to 8 ads, never fewer than 3.
Plan at least 10 ads total per concept across multiple packs.
If the budget cannot fund enough packs, cut packs, not ads per pack.

test.method: Compare delivery evenness and read quality between correctly sized packs and oversized or undersized ones.

title: Give a new pack a short guaranteed-delivery window, then remove it
hypothesis: If a new pack gets a daily minimum delivery floor for its first 7 days, then removed, new ads get a fair chance to be seen instead of being starved by older ads that already hog delivery.

signal.check: Check whether new packs currently get no delivery guarantee and are outcompeted immediately by older, proven ads.

expected_effect.size: ad set daily minimum of 1x target CPA, capped at 20% of budget, removed on day 7

risk.note: Never leave the floor on past 7 days; state the delivery option and the reason in every test plan. This is executed by deployment.

prerequisites: Target CPA and daily budget per pack
steps: Set an ad set daily minimum of 1x target CPA, capped at 20% of the campaign's daily budget.
At very small budgets, use a per-ad impression cap instead so every ad gets equal visibility.
Remove the floor on day 7 and let delivery allocate normally after that.
Check that floors across all packs fit inside the total daily budget before launch.

test.method: Compare delivery evenness in the first 7 days between a floored pack and an unfloored one.

title: Wait at least 7 days before judging a new pack
hypothesis: If no pack is judged before day 7, then early noise from checkout and shipping timing does not get mistaken for a real result.

signal.check: Check whether packs are currently being killed or judged after 1 to 2 days.

expected_effect.size: day 7 is the first read; day 14 is the decision point

risk.note: Reads before day 7 are directional only, not a basis for a kill decision.

steps: Set day 7 as the earliest point for any read.
Set day 14 as the decision point: scale, iterate, or drop.
Treat any earlier signal as directional only, not a kill trigger.

test.method: Compare early (day 2) and later (day 7) reads on the same pack to see how often they disagree.

title: Record a batch with little delivery as inconclusive, not as failed
hypothesis: If ads that received little or no delivery are recorded as inconclusive rather than as losers, then the team reruns them with enough delivery instead of wrongly writing off ideas that were never actually tested.
does_not_apply_when: a pack where every ad received meaningful delivery

signal.check: Check whether ads with almost no spend were marked as failures in the last batch review.

risk.note: Common at small budgets when 30 ads launch with too little spend to reach any of them properly.

steps: Check delivery per ad after the read window.
Mark any ad with near-zero spend as inconclusive, not as a failure.
Rerun fewer creatives with a budget that can actually reach them.

test.method: Track how many 'failed' ads were actually inconclusive by delivery over the last quarter.

title: Exclude existing customers from cold tests and keep winners where they scale
hypothesis: If existing customers are excluded from cold creative tests and a winning ad is scaled by raising its budget rather than relaunching it elsewhere, then cold results stay clean and a proven ad does not lose its accumulated learning.

signal.check: Check whether cold or prospecting campaigns currently include existing customers, or whether a winner was recently turned off and relaunched to 'reset' it.

risk.note: This is a deployment-facing exclusion setting the creative agent should call out in the test plan.

steps: Exclude existing or recent (about 180-day) purchasers from cold and prospecting test audiences.
Scale a winner by raising its budget and adding more ads to its concept in a new ad set.
Never turn a winner off to relaunch it elsewhere.

test.method: Compare new-customer CPA before and after applying the exclusion consistently.

title: Read the full chain: attention, click, post-click, and incremental result
hypothesis: If every ad read checks whether the right people stopped, clicked, did something after the click, and caused sales the business would not otherwise have had, then a creative problem is not confused with a page or offer problem.

signal.check: Check whether ad reads stop at CTR or CPA with no look at post-click or incremental behavior.

risk.note: If quality clicks do not buy, check the landing page before blaming the creative.

prerequisites: Per-ad metrics down to the on-site funnel
steps: Read attention: hook rate or hold rate on video, or CTR on statics.
Read click: CTR against link CTR.
Read post-click: conversion rate, add-to-cart, checkout, page speed, offer, price, and shipping.
Read incremental: whether the ad caused sales the business would not otherwise have had.

test.method: Run this full chain read on the next batch of test results before making a scale or kill decision.

title: Read CTR next to link CTR before trusting a high click-through rate
hypothesis: If CTR is always read alongside link CTR and post-click behavior, then a visually stimulating ad with empty attention is not mistaken for a strong performer.

signal.check: Check whether an ad has high overall CTR but a large drop to link CTR and little buying behind it.

expected_effect.size: one example pair: 10.9% CTR with a drop over 3% and little buying, versus 6.3% CTR with a drop under 2% and real buying

risk.note: Whether the gap is in points or a relative percentage is unclear in the source; check the platform's own column definitions.

prerequisites: CTR and link CTR columns available
steps: Pull both CTR (all) and link CTR for the ad.
Calculate the drop between the two.
Flag a large drop with little downstream buying as empty attention, not a winner.

test.method: Compare conversion outcomes between ads with a small CTR-to-link-CTR gap and ads with a large one.

title: Rank ads by spend first, then require the outcome to hold before calling it a winner
hypothesis: If ads are sorted by amount spent first and then checked against an outcome threshold and a sensible concept reason, then a high-spend ad is not crowned a winner on spend alone, and a genuine opener is not missed either.

signal.check: Check whether the account currently ranks ads by ROAS alone with no reference to how much each has spent.

risk.note: In a very small or weak-pixel account, early spend can reflect early engagement rather than buying intent; watch the ad, not just the sort order.

steps: Sort ads by amount spent.
Require each flagged ad to also clear the outcome threshold, such as CPA or incremental ROAS.
Check the ad makes sense as a concept before calling it a winner.
Watch high-spend, low-ROAS ads for a possible opener role rather than dismissing them.

test.method: Compare the winner list produced by spend-first ranking against a ROAS-only ranking on the same batch.

title: Judge winners on incremental or 7-day-click results at ad set level, not ad-level last click
hypothesis: If winner calls use incremental or 7-day-click results at ad set or campaign level with existing customers excluded, then a top-of-funnel ad is not wrongly killed for a last-click number that a bottom-funnel ad captured instead.

signal.check: Check whether ads are currently being paused based on ad-level last-click ROAS alone.

expected_effect.size: one example: 1.42 reported ROAS versus 1.23 incremental ROAS on the same $97,000

risk.note: Requires incremental attribution availability from deployment; if the gap between reported and incremental is large, check the setup with 24-DEP and 06-MEA before scaling.

prerequisites: Incremental attribution reporting, or 7-day click at ad set level
steps: Switch the primary read to incremental attribution where available, or 7-day click otherwise.
Read at ad set or campaign level, not ad level.
Exclude existing customers from the read.
If incremental and reported results disagree sharply, hold the scale decision and check the attribution setup.

test.method: Compare winner calls made on ad-level last click against calls made on incremental ad-set-level results for the same batch.

title: Write down the winner definition before you launch the test
hypothesis: If the definition of a winner, spend share, CPA threshold, or incremental ROAS bar, is written before the test launches, then the read is not shaped after the fact to fit whatever result came in.

signal.check: Check whether the last test's winner definition was decided only after seeing the results.

expected_effect.size: example bar: spend over 5% of campaign budget at or under target CPA; ads at 1.13 to 1.16 against a 1.1 incremental ROAS bar are left alone

risk.note: Also decide before launch how the ad will be checked for whether it can hold spend at a larger budget.

prerequisites: Target CPA and breakeven incremental ROAS
steps: Before launch, write the spend share, CPA, or incremental ROAS bar that defines a winner.
Write the minimum days required before the definition can be applied.
Leave ads sitting right at the threshold alone rather than forcing a call either way.

test.method: Audit whether the pre-set definition was actually used, unchanged, when results came in.

title: Judge total profit across concepts, not the single best ROAS
hypothesis: If scaling decisions weigh total profit across all profitable concepts instead of chasing the single highest ROAS, then a lower-ROAS ad that can absorb large spend is not cut to feed a high-ROAS ad that can only spend a little.

signal.check: Check whether the account recently cut a profitable, high-spend-capacity ad to shift budget toward a smaller, higher-ROAS ad.

expected_effect.size: example: a 2x return spending $50,000 profitably adds more than a 10x return that can spend only $500

risk.note: Requires contribution margin per order to compute real profit, not just ROAS.

prerequisites: Contribution margin per order
steps: List every concept currently profitable at its own spend level.
Compute total profit contribution across all of them, not just the top ROAS one.
Keep every profitable concept running rather than concentrating spend in the single best performer.

test.method: Model total portfolio profit under a top-ROAS-only strategy versus a run-everything-profitable strategy using last month's data.

title: Keep a weak ad only when the brand's own numbers justify its funnel slot
hypothesis: If a weak-looking ad is kept only when spend, purchases, and margin across several windows justify its funnel slot, then the account avoids both keeping dead weight and cutting a real opener too early.

signal.check: Check whether ads are being kept purely for 'stage coverage' with no supporting numbers, or cut inside an ad set that is otherwise hitting KPI.

risk.note: Never cut an ad inside an ad set that is hitting its KPI target, even if that one ad looks weak alone.

prerequisites: Per-ad spend, purchases, and margin over several windows
steps: Pull spend, purchases, and margin for the ad over several time windows.
Keep it only if those numbers justify its funnel slot.
Do not keep an ad on stage-coverage reasoning alone.
Never cut an ad inside an ad set that is otherwise hitting KPI.

test.method: Review a sample of currently kept weak ads against their real spend, purchase, and margin numbers.

title: Assign each surviving ad a funnel role from its real metrics, not its brief
hypothesis: If each ad's funnel role, opener, closer, or retargeting, is assigned from its combined metrics after launch, then the team catches ads that behave differently from what the brief intended.

signal.check: Check whether an ad's funnel role is still assumed from its original brief with no check against its real spend, ROAS, and scale behavior.

risk.note: A great CPA at a very low daily budget may be a retargeting ad, not a scalable opener.

steps: Pull spend, ROAS, and scale behavior for each surviving ad.
High spend with lower ROAS that still holds at scale suggests an opener role.
Strong conversion at lower spend suggests a closer or retargeting role.
Update the ad's tag to match its real role, not its original brief.

test.method: Recheck funnel role assignments quarterly against updated metrics.

title: Use public ad-library signals only to pick what to study, never to declare a winner
hypothesis: If likes, run time, and ad-library position are used only to shortlist competitor ads for study, then the team does not mistake a weak public proxy for real proof of performance.

signal.check: Check whether a competitor ad's long run time or high likes is being treated as proof it performs well.

risk.note: All 4 sources that use these signals also note their limits.

steps: Use likes, run time, and ad-library position only to decide which competitor ads are worth a closer look.
Never cite these numbers as proof an ad is a winner.
Study the structure, not the implied results, of any long-running competitor ad.

test.method: None; this is a research-discipline rule, not a launchable test.

title: Diagnose fatigue as a small persona pool or a genuinely worn-out ad before acting
hypothesis: If a declining winner is checked for cold frequency above 2 and for whether its persona pool is naturally small, then the team holds spend at capacity for a small niche instead of wrongly scrapping an ad that just needs rotation.

signal.check: Check cold frequency at ad level over 30 and 60 days for a declining winner, and whether reach is falling alongside it.

expected_effect.size: cold frequency above 2 at ad level over 30 or 60 days is the flag

risk.note: Ask a platform rep for the Creative Similarity Score if available; without it, use rising frequency, falling reach, and falling ROAS together as the signal.

prerequisites: Frequency, reach, and ROAS trend per ad
steps: Pull frequency, reach, and ROAS trend for the declining ad over 30 and 60 days.
If frequency is above 2 and reach and ROAS are both falling, treat it as genuine fatigue.
If the persona pool is naturally small, hold spend at its capacity and rotate creative instead of scrapping the concept.

test.method: Track whether ads diagnosed this way respond better to rotation than to being dropped outright.

title: Revive a fatigued winner with new-footage hooks before making new concepts
hypothesis: If a fatigued winner gets new hooks shot as new footage with a different person, changing at least 2 levers, before any new concept is built, then the account gets another run of spend from a proven body at low cost.
does_not_apply_when: a body that has already been revived once and failed to hold even briefly

signal.check: Check whether a proven ad has been declining for months at steady spend with rising frequency, and whether the team has already jumped to building brand-new concepts.

expected_effect.size: one case matched its old spend level and one reached 5x the account average after revival

risk.note: Do not re-cut hooks from the old footage; the market already saw and rejected that opening.

prerequisites: Confirmed fatigue per R151
steps: Keep the proven body unchanged; do not start with a full rework.
Shoot new hooks as new footage with a different presenter.
Change at least 2 levers: angle, offer, avatar, or format.
Produce more than 3 hooks, targeting about 10, launched in budget-sized waves.
Judge against the ad's pre-fatigue baseline at the same daily spend.

test.method: Compare CPA after revival against the ad's pre-fatigue baseline.
test.read_point: After day 7 to 14 of the revival launch

title: Iterate winners with a real swing and keep some net-new concepts every batch
hypothesis: If a winner's iteration keeps the active element and rotates the rest as a genuine swing, and net-new concepts stay part of every batch, then the account keeps building on what works without letting all spend collapse into variants of one ad.

signal.check: Check whether recent 'iterations' were 1-word headline changes or background-color swaps rather than a real swing.

risk.note: Do not drop a winning idea before the market does; watch frequency and reach to see when it has actually fatigued.

prerequisites: A DNA hypothesis for the winner (R157)
steps: From the DNA hypothesis, keep the active element and rotate the rest: hooks, persona, offer, format, or conceit.
Make each iteration a real swing, not a 1-word or color change.
Consider merging 2 proven concepts into a 3rd.
Keep net-new concepts at 20% to 30% of the batch, pulled from the gap matrix.
Launch iterations as a new pack, never into the winning ad set.

test.method: Check that no 2 ads in the new batch are near-identical, and track hit rate by iteration versus net-new.

title: Rotate ad format, not just hooks, when a winner fatigues
hypothesis: If a fatigued winner is rotated to a different format, video to image, VSL to UGC, image to a long-copy static, then it gets a genuinely fresh reach path instead of relying on other tactics that only extend it briefly.

signal.check: Check whether the only fatigue fix tried so far has been new hooks, with no format change attempted.

risk.note: A fatigued ad cannot be saved indefinitely; the real fix is other working ads in the portfolio, not endless rotation of one.

prerequisites: A fatigued winner that has already had a hook revival attempt (R152)
steps: After a hook revival, if fatigue continues, rotate the format entirely.
Turn a video winner into a static, or a VSL into UGC, or an image into a long-copy static.
Avoid simply duplicating the same ad set as a fatigue fix.

test.method: Compare performance of the format-rotated version against continuing hook-only revivals.

title: Keep the portfolio diverse so the platform serves each ad to a different shopper
hypothesis: If the portfolio stays diverse in persona, angle, offer, and format, then delivery serves each ad to a different shopper instead of bundling near-identical ads into one pool and starving the account of fresh reach.

signal.check: Check whether frequency is rising and reach is falling across the account while several live ads look near-identical.

expected_effect.size: identical creative is estimated to help up to about 2 impressions before purchase probability collapses

risk.note: The exact grouping mechanism is described from memory by presenters, not confirmed platform documentation; re-verify periodically.

steps: Check for near-identical ads currently live at the same time.
Diversify persona, angle, offer, or format across the live set.
Ask a platform rep for the Creative Similarity Score if it is available.
Track frequency and reach as diversity increases.

test.method: Compare reach and frequency before and after diversifying a set of near-identical ads.

title: Break every winner and loser into the same parts and write a hypothesis for why
hypothesis: If every winner and the worst loser in a batch are broken into the same fields, segment, concept, mechanism, copy blocks, hook, and format, then the team writes a real, testable hypothesis instead of saying 'it just works'.

signal.check: Check whether the last batch's winner review has any written hypothesis for why it won, or just a performance number.

risk.note: If no hypothesis can be written, test 2 candidate elements in separate packs rather than guessing.

steps: Fill in segment, concept, angle, mechanism, and copy blocks for the winner and the worst loser.
Quote the hook and note the format, and for video, break down conceit, actor, style, terrain, and setup.
Compare winner and loser on the same fields.
Write a hypothesis: is 1 element responsible, or a combination?

test.method: Check whether the next batch's brief references a specific hypothesis from this analysis.

title: Tag the live ad library and look for gaps in a segment-by-format matrix
hypothesis: If the live library is tagged and mapped against a segment-by-format matrix, then a segment buried in comments and reviews but never turned into an ad becomes visible as a real gap for the next batch.

signal.check: Check whether a monthly gap review currently exists, or whether the concept board is built from memory with no matrix.

risk.note: Mark which cells competitors run too, so a format the brand never tried but a rival runs stands out as a gap.

prerequisites: Live ad library tagged by concept, persona, angle, offer, format, and stage
steps: Tag every live ad by segment and format.
Build a matrix marking which segment-format cells are covered and which are empty.
Compare against competitor formats seen in research.
Feed empty cells into the next concept board and volume plan.

test.method: Track how many of the next batch's rows trace to a specific matrix gap.

title: Run a frame-by-frame teardown before deciding what to fix on a live video
hypothesis: If an underperforming video gets a step-by-step, 3-second-chunk teardown covering hook, bridge, body, objections, proof, pace, and CTA, then the real weak point is identified before spending on a re-edit.

signal.check: Check whether a video is being re-edited or paused with no structured teardown first.

risk.note: This is a read, not a prediction of ROAS; do not predict performance from the teardown alone.

prerequisites: Retention curve data if available
steps: Watch the video once, then step through it in 3-second chunks.
Name the hook type and check whether only the target buyer would stop.
Check the bridge for a real solution-exists line versus a direct pitch.
Check when education starts, whether objections are answered, and whether every claim has proof on screen.
Check pace, setting, CTA fit, and click the destination.
Rank the fixes found rather than rewriting the whole script.

test.method: Compare performance of the ad after fixing only the top-ranked issue from the teardown.

title: Study competitor ad libraries for structure only, never for their unproven claims
hypothesis: If competitor ad libraries are studied for layout, hook structure, and pacing rather than for the claims made or the implied results, then the brand gets useful structural ideas without inheriting an unproven or risky claim.

signal.check: Check whether a recent creative idea copied a competitor's specific claim or number along with its structure.

risk.note: Under the competitor-copying override, only layout, structure, and mood may be borrowed; never text, claims, logos, or faces.

prerequisites: Ad library access
steps: Study competitor ads that ship strong creative for their structure, pacing, and layout.
Note the structural pattern separately from any specific claim made.
Rebuild the structure with the brand's own persona, angle, offer, and true, sourced claims.
Never carry over a competitor's specific number, study, or claim.

test.method: None; this is a research and compliance discipline, not a launchable test.

title: Run the creative pipeline in order: research, concept, build, variations, feedback, launch
hypothesis: If the pipeline runs research, concept, build, variations, internal feedback, then launch in that order, then each step has the input it needs, since skipping ahead means the later steps carry no real weight.

signal.check: Check whether the team currently jumps to build or variations before research and concept are done.

risk.note: Variations exist to squeeze a bit more spend through a proven concept, not to replace concept work.

steps: Confirm research and concept are done before any build work starts.
Build the asset from the approved concept.
Add variations only after the core asset is built.
Run internal feedback before launch.

test.method: Audit a sample of recent assets for whether each pipeline step was actually completed in order.

title: Give every brief the same fixed fields so the batch stays diverse
hypothesis: If every brief carries the same fixed fields, concept, creative type, angle, headline, CTA, visual direction, awareness stage, and destination, then the batch stays trackable and does not accidentally produce a hundred versions of the same ad.

signal.check: Check whether briefs currently vary in format from asset to asset with no fixed field set.

risk.note: Always write down the creative type on the brief so the team can see when it is repeating itself.

steps: Create one standard brief template with: concept, creative type, angle, headline, CTA, visual direction.
Add awareness stage, destination, emotion, proof available, claims cleared, and the hypothesis.
Use the same template for every asset in the batch.
Check creative-type diversity across the batch before launch.

test.method: Compare creative-type diversity in a batch built on the standard brief versus a prior batch without it.

title: Use AI in the middle of the pipeline; keep ideation and analysis human
hypothesis: If AI is used for briefing, scripting, and production while ideation and results analysis stay human, then output avoids the generic 'average answer' AI tends to give when it is used to decide strategy.

signal.check: Check whether AI is currently used to generate concepts or analyze results with no human review of the strategy behind it.

expected_effect.size: expect about 50% of AI output to be usable with deep brand context

risk.note: Full automation with no human at concepting or feedback tends to produce generic 'slop' output.

steps: Keep ideation and results analysis as human decisions.
Use AI heavily for briefing, scripting, and production drafts once a human has set the concept.
Review every AI output before it counts toward the batch, expecting about half to need real rework.

test.method: Track usable-output rate from AI-assisted production over a quarter.

title: Load the brand's own facts and past winners into any AI tool before generating
hypothesis: If an AI tool is loaded with the brand book, product facts, allowed claims, personas, and the brand's own winning ads before it generates anything, and never asked to copy a competitor's ad, then its output reflects this brand instead of a generic answer or someone else's ad.

signal.check: Check whether the AI tool currently generates from a brand URL and a short prompt with no deeper context file, or has been asked to copy a competitor ad directly.

risk.note: AI may reuse the brand's own winners and layout ideas; it must never be asked to clone a competitor's ad.

prerequisites: Brand book, claims list, and a file of past winning ads
steps: Assemble a brand book: URL, products, allowed and forbidden claims, personas, brand voice.
Add the brand's own past winning ads to the context.
Connect account data read-only if the tool supports it, so research ranks by real KPIs.
Add over time as the context proves thin in any area.
Never prompt the tool to copy or clone a specific competitor ad.

test.method: Compare usable-output rate before and after loading full brand context.

title: Keep the real product photo in every AI-assisted image
hypothesis: If AI is used to build the scene, illustration, or layout while the product itself stays the real photo, composited in, then buyers get exactly what they saw in the ad, avoiding returns and trust damage from a redrawn product.

signal.check: Check whether an AI-generated image has redrawn the product itself rather than compositing in the real photo.

risk.note: This matters most where accuracy is critical, such as jewelry, apparel detail, or packaging and labels.

prerequisites: Real product photos
steps: Let AI build the scene, background, illustration, or layout.
Composite the real product photo into the generated scene rather than letting AI redraw it.
Check the final image against the real product before launch.

test.method: Compare return rate on ads using a composited real photo against any that used a fully AI-generated product image.

title: Write the hook first, let AI draft the rest, then hand-edit before a human editor cuts video
hypothesis: If the hook is written by a human first, AI drafts the rest, a human hand-edits the mechanism and copy blocks, and a human editor finishes video with a winning reference, then AI speeds up production without taking over the parts that decide whether the ad actually works.

signal.check: Check whether the current workflow lets AI draft the hook itself with no human draft first, or sends AI-drafted video straight to launch with no human editor pass.

risk.note: None; this is a workflow order, not new spend.

steps: Write the hook by hand first.
Let AI draft the body and remaining copy blocks.
Hand-edit the mechanism and copy blocks for accuracy and voice.
Send video to a human editor with a winning reference before finishing.

test.method: Compare usable-output rate between this workflow order and letting AI draft the hook as well.

title: Tag every asset by concept, persona, angle, offer, format, stage, and source
hypothesis: If every asset is tagged by concept, persona, angle, offer, format, awareness stage, and source pillar from the first batch onward, then patterns and coverage gaps become visible instead of staying hidden in an untagged library.

signal.check: Check whether the ad library currently has no consistent tagging system across these fields.

risk.note: Without tags, the gap matrix and the sourcing-mix check both become impossible to run.

steps: Define the tag fields: concept, persona, angle, offer, format, stage, source pillar.
Tag every new asset with these fields starting with the next batch.
Backfill tags on the existing library where practical.
Use the tags to run the gap matrix and sourcing-mix checks.

test.method: Check the percentage of the live library with complete tags each month.

title: Run every health, body, or appearance claim past proof and policy before launch
hypothesis: If every health, weight, body, fertility, or appearance claim is checked against proof and the platform's and market's policy before launch, then the ad avoids a takedown, a rejected campaign, or a false claim reaching customers.

signal.check: Check whether a health, weight, body, fertility, or appearance claim in the current batch has been checked against policy and proof.

risk.note: None of the source presenters actually check this; the check has to be built in deliberately.

prerequisites: Current platform and local market policy for the category
steps: List every health, weight, body, fertility, or appearance claim in the asset.
Check each against current platform policy for the category and local rules for the market.
Record pass, fix, or reject per claim, attached to the test plan.
Also screen for any fake interview, whistleblower, or invented-person format, and confirm rights are cleared for every face and image used.

test.method: None; this is a compliance gate applied before every launch, not a performance test.

title: Replace before-and-after imagery with an illustrated or framed version
hypothesis: If transformation content uses an illustrated route or a 'what life could look like' framing instead of a real before-and-after photo, then the ad reduces its platform policy risk while still showing the transformation idea.

signal.check: Check whether the current asset uses a real before-and-after photo pair in a health, beauty, or body category.

risk.note: Never try to sneak a before-and-after past review; that instruction from a source is explicitly rejected here.

prerequisites: Compliance check on the category
steps: Identify any real before-and-after image pair in the asset.
Replace it with an illustration or a 'what life could look like' framing.
Run the replacement past the compliance check before launch.

test.method: Compare delivery approval and CTR between the illustrated version and the direct-photo version, where policy allows a comparison.

title: Disclose paid partnerships and never present a brand page as independent
hypothesis: If every creator or founder handle used in an ad carries a partnership label and any brand-owned education page discloses it belongs to the brand, then the ad avoids the undisclosed-relationship and fake-independence risk some sources recommend.

signal.check: Check whether a current partnership ad has no partnership label, or whether a brand-owned page presents itself as an independent review site.

risk.note: Undisclosed whitelisting and a brand-owned page presented as independent are explicitly rejected practices here, even though some sources recommend them.

steps: Check every creator or founder handle running a partnership ad for the partnership label.
Check every education page for a clear statement that it belongs to the brand.
Fix any missing disclosure before launch.

test.method: None; this is a compliance gate, not a performance test.

title: Show a generic old way failing instead of naming or showing a competitor
hypothesis: If a comparison ad shows a generic 'old way' failing with true claims instead of naming or showing a specific rival, then the brand gets the persuasive power of a comparison without the legal and platform risk of an unauthorized rival callout.

signal.check: Check whether a current comparison ad names, shows, or stages the failure of a specific competitor's product.

risk.note: Never stage a problem that is not real, even for a generic 'old way' demonstration.

steps: Check the comparison ad for any competitor name, logo, packaging, or recognizable product.
Rewrite it as a generic 'old way' failing, with true, honest claims.
Confirm the demonstrated failure is real, not staged for effect.

test.method: None; this is a compliance gate, not a performance test.

title: Run a policy check on any copy that implies a personal attribute
hypothesis: If any copy implying race, health condition, sexual function, fertility, or body shape is checked against personal-attributes policy before launch, then the ad avoids a rejection or a real harm to how a group is portrayed.

signal.check: Check whether hook or persona copy names a race, health condition, sexual function, fertility status, or body shape with no policy check done.

risk.note: Rewrite or clear before this copy reaches a live ad; do not launch on the assumption it will pass review.

steps: Scan hook and persona copy for any implied personal attribute.
Run flagged copy past the platform's personal-attributes policy for the market.
Rewrite or clear before launch.

test.method: None; this is a compliance gate, not a performance test.

title: Match every scarcity line and price to what is live on the site
hypothesis: If scarcity claims, prices, and dates in an ad are checked against the live store on the day it runs, then the ad never makes a promise checkout cannot keep.

signal.check: Check whether a scarcity line such as 'before stock runs out' or a discount percentage matches what is actually live on the site right now.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one example ran a scarcity line for 20 weeks with no real scarcity

risk.note: This needs a recurring check, not a one-time launch check, since offers and stock levels change.

prerequisites: Current offer and dates from the live store
steps: List every scarcity claim, price, and date in the ad.
Check each against the live store on the day of launch.
Set a recurring check while the ad continues to run.
Fix or remove any line that no longer matches.

test.method: Spot-check live ads monthly against the current site offer.

title: Get consent before calling checkout abandoners for objection research
hypothesis: If checkout-abandoner calls for objection research always start with documented contact consent, then the store gathers real objection data without a consent or privacy violation.

signal.check: Check whether abandoner calls are being made with no consent record and no staff time budgeted for it.

risk.note: Check local consent rules for calling customers in the market before starting this research method.

prerequisites: A consent process and budgeted staff time
steps: Check local consent rules for calling customers in the target market.
Set up a documented consent process before any abandoner calls begin.
Budget staff time for the calls.
Log consent on file for every call made.

test.method: Audit the consent record for the next batch of abandoner calls.

title: Plan creative ramp and clear-down around the store's own peak and gifting occasions
hypothesis: If creative ramp, refresh, and clear-down are planned around the store's own peak and gifting occasions ahead of time, then the store is not scrambling to reword a hook once the period has already started.
does_not_apply_when: a brand with no meaningful seasonal or gifting peak

signal.check: Check whether creative for the last major peak period, such as Black Friday, was planned more than a few weeks ahead or built at the last minute.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source; verify with brand data

risk.note: This folder's sources barely cover seasonality; treat this as an untested hypothesis to verify with the brand's own calendar.

prerequisites: The store's own peak and gifting occasion calendar
steps: List the store's known peak and gifting occasions for the year.
Plan creative ramp-up, refresh, and clear-down dates ahead of each occasion.
Build occasion-specific offer and hook variants ahead of the period, not during it.
Review performance after each occasion to refine next year's calendar.

test.method: Compare performance of pre-planned seasonal creative against last-minute seasonal creative from a prior period.

title: Change one meaningful variable per test and make it big enough to measure
hypothesis: If a test changes one meaningful variable, such as hook, angle, audience, page, or offer, instead of several at once, then the read actually teaches something instead of leaving the team unable to say what caused the result.
does_not_apply_when: an iteration meant purely to produce volume from a winner, which is tagged as iteration, not an attribution test

signal.check: Check whether the last test changed hook, angle, audience, page, and offer all at once with no way to isolate what worked.

risk.note: A rotation meant to produce volume from a winner, changing several parts at once, is fine as iteration; just do not call it an attribution test.

steps: Before launch, name the single variable this test is meant to isolate.
Check the change is big enough to plausibly move the outcome, not a token tweak.
Keep every other element of the ad identical to the control.
Label a multi-variable rotation as iteration, not as a controlled test.

test.method: Review the next 5 tests for whether each one changed a single named variable.

title: Tag every creative with its awareness stage and shopper-journey point
hypothesis: If every ad is tagged by awareness stage and by before-cart, at-cart, at-checkout, or post-purchase, then the team can see coverage gaps instead of guessing where the library is thin.

signal.check: Check the ad library. If ads carry no awareness-stage tag, this idea is live.

risk.note: Tag by how much the ad actually explains, not by what the brief intended.

prerequisites: Live ad export with images or scripts
steps: Classify each live ad as unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware, or most aware.
Tag the shopper-journey point it targets: before cart, at cart, at checkout, or post-purchase.
Store the tag with the ad id in the tagged library.
Re-check the tag against what the ad actually shows, not the brief.

test.method: Tag the full live library once and repeat monthly to track coverage change.

title: Weight new creative at least 70% toward the less-aware stages
hypothesis: If at least 70% of new assets serve unaware, problem aware, or solution aware viewers, then the account stops relying on bottom-of-funnel creative that cannot scale on cold traffic.
does_not_apply_when: a brand with a long consideration cycle that genuinely needs more middle-funnel creative

signal.check: Tag the live library by stage. If most of it sits at product aware or most aware, this idea is live.

expected_effect.size: at least 70% to 90% of new assets at unaware, problem aware, or solution aware

risk.note: Do not build a library that is all testimonials and offers with nothing for cold traffic.

prerequisites: Live ads tagged by stage (R19)
steps: Count the current library's share of assets by stage.
Set a target of at least 70% at the three colder stages for the next batch.
Fill the concept board with cold-stage rows first before adding bottom rows.
Recheck the split after the batch launches.

test.method: Compare account new-customer revenue before and after shifting the stage mix.

title: Keep the hook, image, copy, and destination at the same awareness stage
hypothesis: If every part of an ad, hook, image, copy, and page, is written at the same awareness stage, then the ad stops confusing viewers with a mismatched curiosity hook and feature-tour body.

signal.check: Review a live ad. If the hook implies curiosity but the body jumps into features and specs, this idea is live.

risk.note: None; this is a review discipline, not a build cost.

prerequisites: Stage tags on the concept row (R19)
