steps: Classify the stage of the hook or first image separately from the stage of the body copy.
If they differ, rewrite one so both match.
Repeat the check for the landing page destination.

test.method: A/B a stage-matched ad against the current mismatched version.

title: Choose format after the concept, using the education and demo test
hypothesis: If format is chosen by whether the concept needs education, fits one frame, or needs a demo, then production goes to the cheapest format that can actually carry the concept.

signal.check: Check whether the last brief named the format, such as UGC or static, before the concept was written.

risk.note: If a static fails on an angle that truly needs a demo, retest in video before concluding the angle failed.

prerequisites: A written concept row
steps: Ask whether the concept needs education; if yes, plan a VSL, long video, or long-copy static.
Ask whether the value fits in one frame; if yes, lean to a static or carousel.
Ask whether the product needs a demo; if yes, plan video.
Ask what stage the ad serves and match format length to it.
Record the format and the reason on the concept row.

test.method: Compare a format-matched ad against one produced in the team's default format.

title: Test new angles and offers as statics before building video
hypothesis: If a new angle or offer is tested as a static first, then the store learns which ideas work at a fraction of video's cost before committing to a shoot.

signal.check: Check whether the last new angle went straight to video production without a cheaper static test.

expected_effect.size: statics run about 4x cheaper to produce than video in the source's example

risk.note: A static cannot show a value that must be seen moving; move those concepts straight to video.

steps: For each new angle or offer, build a static version first.
Launch the static test before committing to a video shoot for the same concept.
If the static wins, decide whether to turn the angle into video for further scale.
Skip this step only when the concept needs a visible demo.

test.method: Compare cost per learning between a static-first sequence and a video-first sequence.

title: Compare formats by expected gross profit per ad, not by ROAS alone
hypothesis: If the team compares formats on revenue per ad minus spend per ad minus production cost, then a cheap static that returns less ROAS but more profit is not dropped in favor of an expensive video.
does_not_apply_when: a brand with no per-ad production cost data yet

signal.check: Check whether production mix decisions are made on ROAS alone with no production cost in the math.

expected_effect.size: worked example: at 10x return, a $20 static nets 20.5% more profit than a $200 video on the same $1,000 revenue

risk.note: Requires real per-ad production cost and revenue data; without it this is a rough estimate.

prerequisites: Revenue, spend, and production cost by ad and format
steps: Pull average revenue per ad, average spend per ad, and production cost per ad by format.
Compute expected gross profit per ad: revenue minus spend minus production cost.
Rank formats by this figure, not by ROAS alone.
Shift the next production plan toward the higher gross-profit format.

test.method: Run the calculation on last quarter's data and compare the ranked list against the current production mix.

title: Stop putting cold budget behind product-aware creative
hypothesis: If product-aware creative such as testimonials and price call-outs is kept out of cold campaigns, then cold spend goes to ads that can actually educate an unaware viewer.

signal.check: Check what creative is running in cold or prospecting campaigns. If it is mostly testimonials, value call-outs, or offers, this idea is live.

risk.note: None; this is a reallocation, not new production.

prerequisites: Creative tagged by stage (R19)
steps: List which creative is currently running in cold or prospecting campaigns.
Move product-aware creative such as testimonials and price call-outs to retargeting.
Replace it in cold with problem-aware or solution-aware creative.

test.method: Compare cold campaign CPA before and after the swap.

title: Build one bottom-of-funnel ad per objection, not a benefit list
hypothesis: If each retargeting or product-aware ad handles one objection with one proof point, then it converts better than an ad trying to cover every objection at once.

signal.check: Check the current retargeting ads. If they list many benefits instead of answering one specific objection, this idea is live.

risk.note: Get consent before calling checkout abandoners to gather objections.

prerequisites: Objection list from surveys, tickets, and reviews
steps: List objections from surveys, tickets, reviews, and, with consent, abandoner calls.
Estimate the mix, for example price, trust, quality doubt, and not-ready.
Build one ad per objection with one proof point, no benefit list.
Load these into a separate bottom-of-funnel pack from top-of-funnel creative.

test.method: Compare a single-objection ad against the current multi-benefit retargeting ad.

title: Check the category's ad library before reusing a native-looking format
hypothesis: If the team scans the category's ad library before building a native-looking format such as a tweet screenshot or notepad style, then it avoids a format the category has already worn out.

signal.check: The last format used was copied from a competitor without checking how long it has run in that category.

risk.note: Format innovation gives only a temporary edge; competitors copy a winning format quickly.

prerequisites: Ad library access
steps: Search the category's ad library for the format being considered.
Check how many brands are already running it and how long it has run.
Treat a format older than about 6 months in the category as saturated until tested.
Prefer a format the category has not used yet, adjacent to proven demand.

test.method: Compare hook rate of a fresh format against a saturated one in the same category.

title: State the click destination on every brief and confirm it matches the offer
hypothesis: If every brief states whether the ad lands on an educational page, the PDP, or the cart, and that page is confirmed live, then the ad's promise and the landing page's job stay congruent.

signal.check: Check the last 5 briefs for a stated destination. If the destination was decided after launch or never checked live, this idea is live.

risk.note: If a curiosity static underperforms on a PDP, test the educational page before concluding the static failed.

prerequisites: Which landing pages exist and their conversion rates
steps: State the destination and its job on every brief: educational page, PDP, or cart.
Send curiosity, native, and advertorial clicks to an educational page, not the PDP.
Send clear-offer statics for product-aware or most-aware buyers to the PDP.
Click the live ad after launch and confirm the page loads and matches the offer.

test.method: A/B the same static to an educational page versus straight to the PDP.

title: Add fit, sizing, and returns risk to the objection list for apparel
hypothesis: If fit, sizing, and returns risk are added to the bottom-of-funnel objection list, then an apparel store's retargeting creative covers the objection that most often blocks a purchase.
does_not_apply_when: a store that does not sell apparel or footwear

signal.check: Check whether fit or sizing appears anywhere in the current objection-handling ad set.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source names a figure

risk.note: Verify this against the brand's own return reasons before treating it as a top objection.

prerequisites: Return reason data or size-related support tickets
steps: Pull return reasons and support tickets for size or fit complaints.
Add a fit or sizing objection ad with its own proof, such as a size chart or fit guide.
Load it into the bottom-of-funnel pack alongside price and trust objection ads.

test.method: Compare return rate on shoppers who saw a fit objection ad against those who did not.

title: Decide the click destination before the format for marketplace-heavy sellers
hypothesis: If a marketplace-heavy seller decides the click destination first, marketplace listing, brand page, or a new lander, then the format choice can actually support that destination instead of assuming an owned PDP exists.
does_not_apply_when: a brand with a strong owned PDP or lander already

signal.check: Check whether the brand has an owned PDP or lander for the products being advertised.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source; verify with brand data

risk.note: Building a lander first can delay a launch; the marketplace listing may be the faster interim destination.

prerequisites: A decision on which pages exist for the product
steps: Check whether an owned PDP or educational page exists for the advertised product.
If not, decide whether to route to the marketplace listing or build a lander first.
Only after that, choose the ad format to match the chosen destination.

test.method: Compare conversion rate between the marketplace listing and a new lander for the same ad.

title: Run several distinct ad formats at once, not just one
hypothesis: If the account runs 10 to 15 distinct formats and angles at once, then delivery shows different formats to different people, reaching viewers a single format never would.
does_not_apply_when: a very small account that cannot yet support more than 1 or 2 formats

signal.check: Count the live formats in the account. If only 1 or 2 formats carry most of the spend, this idea is live.

risk.note: Format still ranks below persona, angle, and offer as a lever; do not use format variety as a substitute for concept variety.

prerequisites: Tagged live ad library
steps: Count how many distinct formats and angles are currently live.
List format families not yet tried: statics, UGC, founder, VSL, native short-form, animation.
Add at least one new format family to the next batch.
Track format count monthly toward the 10 to 15 target.

test.method: Track reach and frequency as format count rises.

title: Shift a lifestyle-heavy brand from mostly desire-led toward more pain-led creative
hypothesis: If a brand built on campaign-style shoots moves its creative mix from about 90% desire-led toward 60% to 70% pain-led performance creative, then cold campaigns get more ads that actually agitate a problem instead of only showing lifestyle imagery.
does_not_apply_when: a brand already running mostly pain-led performance creative

signal.check: Tag the live library as desire-led or pain-led. If it sits near 90% desire and 10% pain, this idea is live.

expected_effect.size: shift from about 90/10 desire-to-pain toward 60/40 to 70/30 pain-led

risk.note: This is one agency's single-source figure; verify against the brand's own account results.

prerequisites: Live library tagged as desire-led or pain-led
steps: Tag each live ad as desire-led or pain-led.
Calculate the current split.
Add pain-led, performance-style rows to the next concept board until the split moves toward 60/40 or 70/30.

test.method: Compare cold CPA before and after the mix shifts.

title: Give every static three jobs: stop the scroll, say the message, drive the click
hypothesis: If every static is built to stop the scroll, communicate the angle and offer, and drive one action, then it does not rely on the image alone to carry the whole sale.

signal.check: Review a static. If it is missing a clear scroll-stopper, a clear message, or a clear next action, this idea is live.

risk.note: None; this is a review checklist, not new spend.

steps: Check the static stops the scroll, either by looking native or by a deliberate pattern interrupt.
Check it communicates the angle, offer, and who it is for in few words, or lets primary text carry it.
Check it drives one action, either hinting at an article behind the click or walking the reader through stages.

test.method: Score a batch of statics against the 3 jobs before launch and compare CTR of high scorers against low scorers.

title: Pick clarity or curiosity for every static; never sit in the middle
hypothesis: If every static is pushed to a clear end, where the offer is obvious in seconds, or a curiosity end, where the viewer must click to learn more, then it avoids the vague middle that reads as a slogan and drives nothing.

signal.check: Read a static's headline. If it sounds like a slogan such as 'guaranteed results' with no clear offer and no real curiosity gap, this idea is live.

risk.note: A curiosity gap only works if the target buyer wants it closed for their own benefit.

steps: Decide which end the static should sit at before writing headline copy.
For the clarity end, make sure product, angle, who it's for, and offer are clear within 3 to 4 seconds.
For the curiosity end, withhold the product and open one loop the target buyer cares about.
Push any middle-ground draft to one end or drop it.

test.method: Compare a clarity-end version and a curiosity-end version of the same concept against the current middle-ground ad.

title: Design the eye path so the highest-awareness message lands first
hypothesis: If the biggest, most contrasted element on a static shows the problem or persona call-out instead of the product category, then a cold viewer does not read the ad as a bottom-funnel pitch at first glance.

signal.check: Glance at the static for 1 second. If the biggest text reads as the product category name, this idea is live.

risk.note: None; this is a layout fix.

steps: Glance at the static for 1 second and note what it says.
If it reads as the product category, replace the biggest element with the problem, persona call-out, or 'new technology' framing.
Plan 3 to 4 eye stops that each answer the last stop's question.
Use size, contrast, and whitespace to control the order the eye follows.

test.method: Compare hook rate between the redesigned eye path and the original.

title: Pair image and headline as one unit and run the substitution test
hypothesis: If the image and headline are written together and pass the substitution test, swapping in a generic image breaks the headline, then the pair carries more meaning than either alone.

signal.check: Swap the static's image for a generic category photo in your head. If the headline still makes sense, the pair is too loose.

risk.note: None; this is a design review step.

steps: Write the headline and choose the image together, not separately.
Mentally swap in a plain, generic category photo.
If the headline still makes sense with the generic photo, rewrite the pair as one unit.
Avoid generic category shots with no link to the headline.

test.method: Compare CTR on a substitution-test-passing static against the previous loosely paired version.

title: Give primary text and headline equal weight to the image on statics
hypothesis: If a static gives little away in the image, the primary text can carry the education and sell, especially on native and advertorial statics where the message must be read, not just seen.

signal.check: Check whether the primary text on the last native static is empty or just repeats the image.

risk.note: Truncation by placement can hide long primary text; verify how it displays before launch.

steps: Write the primary text as a full block, not an afterthought, on native and curiosity-end statics.
Put the product name and offer in the primary text, not the image, on a native static.
Check how the text truncates by placement before launch.

test.method: Compare conversion rate between a static with a written primary text block and one with minimal text.

title: Fix layout faults that break trust, without treating design as the performance lever
hypothesis: If poor spacing, a stray logo, an unreadable graph, or text too small for a phone are fixed, then the static stops losing authority, even though design polish itself does not drive performance.

signal.check: View the static at phone size. If sub-headlines are hard to read, spacing is off, or there is an unneeded logo, this idea is live.

expected_effect.size: enlarge unreadable sub-headlines by about 30% and move them up

risk.note: Some of the best-performing ads look rough; do not chase polish for its own sake, only fix faults that break clarity or trust.

steps: View the static at phone size.
Check spacing, alignment, case consistency, and whether the product is centered.
Enlarge unreadable sub-headlines by about 30% and move them up.
Cut any graph or chart that cannot be read in 2 seconds.
Remove an unneeded corner logo unless it is part of a deliberate native reveal.

test.method: Compare CTR before and after fixing layout faults on the same concept.

title: Lead with the plain benefit; put the mechanism after it in smaller type
hypothesis: If the plain benefit comes first and the mechanism or spec follows in brackets or smaller type, then cold scrollers understand the ad before deciding whether the science matters to them.

signal.check: Read the headline. If it leads with a mechanism or spec term before stating the plain benefit, this idea is live.

risk.note: Specs still matter for product-aware or expert buyers; do not delete them, just reorder.

steps: Identify the plain benefit and the mechanism or spec behind it.
Write the benefit first in the main line.
Move the mechanism or spec into brackets or smaller type after it.
Repeat this order check for video scripts using the same claim.

test.method: A/B a benefit-first version against a mechanism-first version of the same claim.

title: Keep product-shot headlines to 5 or 6 words that beat the current alternative
hypothesis: If a clean product-shot static's headline is cut to 5 to 6 words that answer why this instead of what the buyer uses now, then it stops sounding like a generic promise a substitute could also make.

signal.check: Count the words in the last product-shot headline and check whether a competing product could claim the same line.

expected_effect.size: 5 to 6 word headline on a clean product-shot layout

risk.note: Single-source figure; test against the account's own headline length history.

prerequisites: Real unit price and substitute price if using a savings claim
steps: Write the headline to answer 'why this instead of what they use now'.
Cut it to about 5 to 6 words.
Check whether a substitute product could honestly claim the same line; if so, rewrite it.
Reuse the same clean layout for the next angle, changing only the headline.

test.method: A/B a 5-to-6-word headline against the account's current longer headline on the same product shot.

title: Name the persona and problem in a hook, or list 2 to 3 related problems to widen it
hypothesis: If a hook names a persona and problem in as few words as possible, or lists 2 to 3 related problems, then it self-selects the right reader while widening the pool beyond one narrow condition.
does_not_apply_when: a health-adjacent claim that has not passed the compliance check

signal.check: Check whether the current hook names only 1 narrow condition where 2 to 3 related ones would widen relevance.

risk.note: Health-condition lists carry personal-attribute and claim risk; run the compliance check before launch.

prerequisites: Compliance check on any named condition
steps: Write the persona and problem call-out in as few words as possible.
If one condition is too narrow, list 2 to 3 related problems that widen relevance.
Run the list past the compliance check for health or personal-attribute claims.

test.method: A/B a single-condition hook against a 2-to-3-condition hook on the same body.

title: Make proof recognizable and product shots true to what arrives at home
hypothesis: If a review line carries stars or a name and the product shot matches what arrives at home, then the static builds trust and does not create returns from a surprised buyer.

signal.check: Check whether any review text in a static lacks attribution, or whether a product shot looks better than the real item.

risk.note: A plain, true-to-life product shot can add useful friction so buyers are not surprised on delivery.

prerequisites: Real product photos
steps: Add stars, a name, or a face to any review line used as proof.
Use a true-to-life product shot, not an idealized or staged one.
Compare the shot against the real product before launch.

test.method: Compare return rate on ads using a true-to-life shot against ads using an idealized shot.

title: Never invent a number, study, count, or prevalence figure in an ad
hypothesis: If every number in an ad traces to a real document, order data, or test the brand can show, then the store avoids the platform and legal risk of an unsupported claim, even when a made-up figure would read as more authoritative.

signal.check: List every number in the ad and try to find its source document. Any number with no source is this idea live.

risk.note: An unsupported number, even a small one, can trigger a platform or regulatory flag.

prerequisites: Substantiation for every number the brand wants to use
steps: List every number, percentage, or count used in the ad.
Find the source document, test, or order data behind each one.
Remove any number with no source, even if it 'suggests' authority.
For a true, sourced prevalence line, cite the source in the compliance record.

test.method: Run this check on every asset before launch as a pass or fail gate.

title: Do not send a plain white-background product shot to cold traffic
hypothesis: If cold statics show the problem or the value instead of a plain catalog-style product shot, then they give a cold viewer a reason to click instead of reading as a thumbnail nobody asked for.
does_not_apply_when: a high-intent buyer already comparing where to purchase

signal.check: Check the creative running in cold or prospecting campaigns for a plain product-on-white image.

risk.note: A plain product shot still works for most-aware buyers already deciding who to buy from.

steps: Audit cold campaign creative for plain product-on-white shots.
Replace them with an image that shows the problem, the persona, or the value.
Keep plain product shots only for most-aware or comparison-stage placements.

test.method: Compare CTR of a problem-led image against a plain product shot in the same cold campaign.

title: Write long primary text or build an educational page for unaware statics
hypothesis: If an unaware or problem-aware static pairs a light image with long primary text or an educational page, then the ad can educate even though a static is consumed in about 4 seconds.

signal.check: Check whether cold statics rely only on the image with a short caption and no story or educational path.

risk.note: This format fits older or Facebook-feed audiences best; test before assuming it fits every platform.

prerequisites: A custom lander per angle, or a strong primary text block
steps: Open with a persona or problem call-out in the first line.
Write a first-person story style narrative explaining why the problem happens.
Reveal the product late, with proof and timelines.
Send the click to a custom lander per angle if one exists.

test.method: A/B a long-copy story static against the current short-caption static.

title: Use an illustration instead of a graphic photo for sensitive problems
hypothesis: If a hard-to-photograph or unpleasant problem is shown as an illustration instead of a graphic photo, then the ad can show the problem clearly while lowering the risk of a delivery or policy issue.

signal.check: Check whether a sensitive health or body topic is currently shown with a graphic real photo.

risk.note: Still needs a policy check for the category before launch.

prerequisites: Compliance check on the topic
steps: Identify sensitive or unpleasant-to-photograph topics in the concept board.
Commission an illustration that shows the problem cleanly instead of a graphic real photo.
Run the illustration past the compliance check before launch.

test.method: Compare delivery and CTR of an illustrated version against a graphic-photo version.

title: Scale a proven static by swapping one concept element, not the whole format
hypothesis: If a working static's format and messaging are kept fixed and only one concept element such as product, persona, or category is swapped, then the team scales proven structure faster than rebuilding from scratch each time.

signal.check: Check whether a proven static format has been left unused for a new product or persona instead of being reused.

risk.note: Only swap words and picture; do not keep iterating the format itself once it is proven.

prerequisites: A static format that has already proven itself in the account
steps: Identify a static format that has already spent well in the account.
Build the layout as a reusable template.
Swap only the words and the product picture for the next persona, product, or category.
Keep the layout, hierarchy, and structure fixed.

test.method: Compare production time and hit rate of template-swapped ads against fully rebuilt ads.

title: Drop the corner logo unless it is part of a deliberate native reveal
hypothesis: If the corner logo is removed when the page name already shows the brand, then the static stays clean and native-looking, except where the logo is the deliberate way a native static reveals itself as an ad.

signal.check: Check statics for cold traffic for an unnecessary corner logo.

risk.note: Keep the logo when it is the intended way the ad reveals itself, such as a light paparazzi-style reveal.

steps: Check whether the page name already shows the brand.
If so, remove the corner logo from the static for cold traffic.
Keep the logo only where it is the deliberate reveal mechanism of a native-style static.

test.method: A/B a logo-removed version against the current logoed static.

title: Do not judge top-of-funnel statics by last-click ROAS
hypothesis: If top-of-funnel statics are judged on account-level new-customer volume and MER instead of their own last-click ROAS, then a cheap-click static is not wrongly killed for a low ad-level number.

signal.check: Check whether a static was paused for low ROAS without checking account-level new-customer revenue around its launch.

risk.note: Requires blended revenue and new-customer data at account level, not just ad-level ROAS.

prerequisites: Blended revenue, new customer count, and MER around launch windows
steps: Before pausing a top-of-funnel static for low ROAS, check account-level new-customer revenue and MER around its launch.
Compare that trend against the period before the static launched.
Only pause it if the account-level signal also weakens.

test.method: Track account MER for 2 weeks after launching a new top-of-funnel static.

title: Test dropping the CTA button copy on a convincing native static
hypothesis: If a strong native-looking static is tested with no added CTA in the image, then it may still convert because a convincing post reads as content that people naturally want to act on.

signal.check: Check whether every static currently forces a CTA overlay even on ads meant to look like organic content.

risk.note: Test, do not assume; a weaker native static may need the CTA to convert.

prerequisites: A native-style static candidate
steps: Pick a native-looking static that already reads as organic content.
Build a version with no CTA overlay in the image.
Launch it against the standard CTA version as a small test.

test.method: A/B the no-CTA-overlay version against the standard version.

title: Judge a competitor's static on its own merit, not on the size of its logo
hypothesis: If a competitor static is judged separately from the weight its brand name carries, then the team avoids copying a mediocre ad that only works because a big brand's logo is attached to it.

signal.check: The team is about to copy a competitor ad's structure without checking whether that brand's size, not the ad, explains its run time.

risk.note: A new, unsaturated category can let a mediocre ad win until rivals arrive; do not read that as proof of quality.

prerequisites: Ad library access for the swipe
steps: When reviewing a competitor swipe, note the brand's size and recognition separately from the ad's structure.
Judge the layout, hook, and copy on their own merit, not on how long the ad has run.
Skip swipes from brands too large or too small to compare with the brand's own size.

test.method: None; this is a research judgment step, not a launchable test.

title: Flag catalog and DPA creative risks before handing off to deployment
hypothesis: If the creative agent flags a bottom-funnel-only catalog layer and the risk of DPA ROAS looking strong on last click but failing an incremental read, then the deployment team catches these before scaling spend on them.
does_not_apply_when: a single-SKU hero product store that runs no catalog or DPA layer

signal.check: Check whether the catalog or DPA layer is treated only as a bottom-funnel afterthought with no incremental read.

risk.note: A hero-SKU store can skip this rule.

prerequisites: Access to incremental attribution reporting, or a plan to get it with 24-DEP
steps: Note whether the catalog layer is being used only as a bottom-funnel afterthought.
Flag the DPA layer for an incremental read, not just last-click ROAS.
Add both flags to the test plan handed to the deployment agent.

test.method: Compare last-click DPA ROAS against incremental ROAS once deployment can run the read.
test.read_point: After deployment runs the incremental comparison

title: Spec creative vertical-only with dual-language hooks for mobile-first markets
hypothesis: If creative for a mobile-first, lower-bandwidth market is built vertical-only and planned with non-English or dual-language hooks, then it fits how that market actually watches ads instead of assuming a desktop or English-only viewer.
does_not_apply_when: a desktop-heavy or English-only market

signal.check: Check whether current creative is built in a square or horizontal aspect ratio, or in English only, for a mobile-first market.

expected_effect.size: unknown, no library source; verify with brand data

risk.note: Legibility at phone size is the only mobile rule this folder's sources cover in detail; the rest is general practice.

prerequisites: Confirmation of the market's primary language and device mix
steps: Confirm the market's primary device is mobile and its bandwidth constraints.
Build creative vertical-only for that market.
Plan a dual-language or local-language hook version alongside the English version.
Check text legibility at phone size before launch.

test.method: Compare hook rate between a vertical local-language version and a horizontal English-only version.

title: Script cold video in order: hook, bridge, mechanism, product, proof, objection, CTA
hypothesis: If a cold video runs hook, bridge, education, mechanism, product, proof, objection handling, then CTA, then the script does not skip the steps that build trust before asking for the sale.

signal.check: Read a cold video script. If it jumps from hook straight to the product pitch with no bridge or education, this idea is live.

risk.note: The order of parts can flex; the parts themselves should not be skipped.

prerequisites: A concept row with mechanism and proof; objections from research
steps: Write the hook naming the viewer's problem, with no product name or offer.
Bridge into education: a solution exists, then why the problem happens.
Explain the mechanism, then reveal the product blended in.
Stack proof and handle at least one real objection.
Close with a reason to buy, risk reversal, and a clear CTA.

test.method: Compare hold rate and CPA on a full-skeleton script against the current script structure.

title: Bridge to education before naming the product, not straight to the pitch
hypothesis: If the bridge after the hook says a solution exists and teaches why the problem happens, instead of naming the product and its benefits, then viewers do not drop at the point most cold ads break.

signal.check: Watch the retention curve right after the hook. A steep drop right after the hook often means the bridge pitched too early.

risk.note: None; this is a script rewrite, not new production.

steps: Read the line right after the hook.
If it names the product and its benefits, rewrite it to say a solution exists and start teaching why the problem happens.
Add a research or supplier story before the product name if the bridge still feels abrupt.

test.method: A/B a rewritten bridge against the current script on the same hook and body.

title: Keep product awareness near zero through the hook, rising slowly to the CTA
hypothesis: If the product name and image stay out of the hook and rise slowly through the body to peak at the CTA, then cold video keeps fewer but more qualified viewers instead of tipping its hand early.
does_not_apply_when: a demo format, a product-aware or retargeting ad, or a partnership ad on an influencer's page

signal.check: Check whether the product name or image appears in the first 3 seconds of a cold video ad.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one example reveals the product at about 1.5 minutes

risk.note: This is a conflict point in the sources; test early versus late reveal in the brand's own account before treating it as fixed.

steps: Check the first 3 seconds of the script for the product name or image.
Remove it if the ad is meant for a cold, education-led audience.
Let product awareness rise slowly through the body.
Peak the product's presence only at the CTA.
Run one early-vs-late reveal test per quarter and record the result.

test.method: A/B a product-late version against a product-early version of the same script.
test.read_point: After day 7, quarterly for the standing test

title: Explain the mechanism at the depth the stage needs before naming the product
hypothesis: If the script explains what the mechanism is and why it fails for problem-aware viewers, or reinforces and differentiates it for solution-aware viewers, then the claim lands at the depth the viewer actually needs instead of assuming too much or too little knowledge.

signal.check: Check whether the script asserts a cause, such as a biological or design reason, without explaining why it matters.

risk.note: None; this is a script depth check.

prerequisites: The stage this ad targets (R19)
steps: Confirm the awareness stage the ad targets.
For problem-aware viewers, explain what the mechanism is and why it causes the problem.
For solution-aware viewers, reinforce the mechanism and explain how the product differs.
Give every ingredient or feature its own reason it matters.

test.method: Compare hold rate between a depth-matched script and the current script.

title: Make the claim, then show the proof immediately after it
hypothesis: If every claim in voiceover, copy, or overlay is followed at once by a shot that proves it, then the ad stops relying on assertions the viewer has no reason to believe.

signal.check: List the claims in the script. If any has no shot, overlay, or number attached, this idea is live.

risk.note: None beyond the shoot cost of the extra proof shot.

prerequisites: Real test results, lab photos, or footage proving the claim
steps: List every claim in the script.
For each, write the shot that proves it, such as a real test result, a demo, or a number on screen.
Cut any claim that has no available proof shot.

test.method: Compare conversion rate on a proof-backed script against the same script with claims left unproven.

title: Handle at least one real objection from customer data before the CTA
hypothesis: If every cold video answers at least one real objection sourced from reviews, tickets, or calls before the CTA, then the ad removes a known blocker instead of hoping the viewer buys anyway.

signal.check: Check whether the script handles any specific objection, or just lists benefits.

risk.note: A very specific objection story can narrow the audience; use it only when that group is large enough.

prerequisites: Objection list from research (R14)
steps: Pull the top objections from reviews, tickets, and survey data.
Write one objection into the script with a real answer before the CTA.
Say what buyers already tried and why it failed, where relevant.

test.method: A/B a version with an explicit objection answered against the current version with none.

title: Say the benefit first, the feature second, and move fast through table stakes
hypothesis: If the script states the benefit before the feature and covers table-stakes features quickly, then cold viewers stay with the ad instead of losing interest during a feature list.

signal.check: Check whether the script leads with a feature name before saying what it does for the viewer.

risk.note: Keep any legally required feature statement even if it slows the read.

steps: List each feature mentioned in the script.
Rewrite each line to state the benefit first, then the feature.
Give table-stakes features, such as standard certifications, one quick line, not a full section.

test.method: Compare hold rate between a benefit-first script and the current feature-first script.

title: Stack proof after the product and match it to the viewer
hypothesis: If proof such as trial results, customer counts, and testimonials appears right after the product reveal and matches the viewer's age and profile, then the close feels earned instead of buried or mismatched.

signal.check: Check where proof appears in the script relative to the product reveal, and whether the people shown in testimonials look like the target persona.

risk.note: Weak or buried proof is a common and easy fix for an underperforming script.

prerequisites: Real testimonials and trial data matched to the persona
steps: Move all proof elements to right after the product reveal.
Match testimonial talent to the target persona's age and profile.
Cut any proof that is generic or does not match the viewer.

test.method: Compare conversion on a matched-and-stacked proof version against the current version.

title: Give a reason to buy, a risk reversal, and a CTA with no open loops
hypothesis: If the close gives a reason to move from learning to buying, a risk reversal, and a clear CTA with no new open loop, then the ad does not lose the viewer right at the finish line.

signal.check: Watch the last 20% of the script. If it jumps from education straight to the offer, or opens a new curiosity loop, this idea is live.

risk.note: None; this is a script rewrite of the closing section.

steps: Read the last 20% of the script.
Add a stated reason to move from learning to buying.
Add a risk reversal, such as a guarantee or trial period.
Close with a clear, single CTA and check no new curiosity loop is left open.

test.method: A/B the rewritten close against the current close on the same body.

title: Match the CTA's intensity to the tone and the work the ad has already done
hypothesis: If the CTA's intensity, soft or hard, matches the ad's tone and how much education and objection handling came before it, then the close does not feel jarring or add friction to a weak script.

signal.check: Check whether a hard pitch is bolted onto a soft, creator-style ad, or a soft close sits on a script with no real education.

risk.note: Scarcity language should only be used when it is actually true.

steps: Classify the ad's tone as soft, creator-style, or hard, direct-response style.
Match the CTA's intensity to that tone.
Check any scarcity claim, such as limited stock, against the live store before keeping it.

test.method: A/B a matched-intensity CTA against a mismatched one on the same script.

title: Fix the opening of an underperforming video before touching the back half
hypothesis: If the first half of a script is fixed before the second half, then a weak ad gets a real chance, because a strong first half can carry an average second half but not the reverse.

signal.check: Check the retention curve. If most drop-off happens in the first half, this idea is live.

expected_effect.size: an estimated 15% of viewers reach the second half

risk.note: Single-source estimate; use the account's own retention curve as the real guide.

prerequisites: Retention curve per ad
steps: Pull the retention curve for the underperforming ad.
Diagnose hook, bridge, and body separately and name the weakest segment.
Keep the strong segments and build a variant that changes only the weakest one.

test.method: Compare the retention curve of the new variant against the original.

title: Edit every video with visible motion; match cut pace to the format's polish
hypothesis: If a polished format cuts at least every 3 seconds and a lo-fi native format still keeps props, handheld moves, and on-screen text, then a shopper scrolling on their phone keeps watching instead of reading the ad as skippable content.

signal.check: Scrub the timeline. If a stretch runs over 3 seconds with no visual change on a polished format, or a lo-fi ad sits completely still, this idea is live.

expected_effect.size: at least every 3 seconds for polished formats

risk.note: Keep the product itself in high-end shots even when the opening footage is deliberately low-fi on a premium brand.

steps: Scrub the current cut for stretches with no visual change.
For polished formats, add a cut, overlay, or camera move at least every 3 seconds.
For lo-fi native formats, add props, handheld movement, or on-screen text instead of hard cuts.
Keep the product only in high-end shots if the opening is deliberately low-fi.

test.method: Compare hold rate between the re-edited version and the original cut.

title: Sell the category or borrow authority when the brand has no famous face
hypothesis: If an unfamiliar or category-defining product leans on category history, licensed names, or design origin for authority, then it earns credibility it cannot get from a founder or influencer face.
does_not_apply_when: a commodity product that looks like its rivals, where origin claims will not move buyers

signal.check: Check whether the brand has a genuine category story, licensed name, or design origin it is not currently using in ads.

risk.note: This depends heavily on era and culture; test before assuming it works for every market.

prerequisites: A true category history or design-origin fact
steps: Confirm the brand has a real category history, licensed relationship, or design origin fact.
Write a script or static that leads with that authority.
Test it against the brand's current founder or influencer-led ad.

test.method: A/B a category-authority version against the founder or influencer-led version.

title: Run the swap-the-face test before scaling a founder or influencer ad on cold
hypothesis: If a founder or influencer ad passes the swap-the-face test, working even with a different person in it, then it is safe to scale on cold; if it only works because of the face, it should stay organic instead.

signal.check: Ask whether the ad's argument would still work with a different presenter.

risk.note: None; this is a diagnostic question, not a build cost.

steps: Watch the founder or influencer ad and ask if it would still work with a different person delivering it.
If the answer is no, it only converts people who already trust that face.
Post that ad organically instead of scaling it on cold spend.
If the answer is yes, scale it on cold as normal.

test.method: Compare cold CPA of ads that pass the swap-the-face test against ads that fail it.

title: Click the live ad's destination before and after every launch
hypothesis: If someone actually clicks the live ad and checks the page loads and holds the ad's promise, then the store avoids losing paid clicks to a broken link or a page that does not continue the ad's story.

signal.check: Check when the last ad's destination was actually clicked and reviewed, not just assumed to work.

risk.note: None; this is a QA step.

steps: Click the live ad's destination before launch and confirm it loads.
Check the page continues the ad's mechanism, story, and offer.
Repeat the click check on a schedule after launch, not just once.

test.method: Log broken or mismatched destinations found on a weekly click-check schedule.

title: Use a numbered-reasons body for routine, consumable products
hypothesis: If a consumable product's ad uses a curiosity hook answered by 3 numbered reasons, felt benefit, table-stakes value, and the main objection, then it fits a routine purchase decision better than a long educational script.
does_not_apply_when: a complex or high-consideration product that needs real education

signal.check: Check whether a consumable product's ads currently run a long educational script when a fast numbered format could work.

risk.note: Only one source names this format; test before adopting it broadly.

steps: Open with a curiosity hook that promises an answer.
Answer it within seconds using a 'here are 3 reasons' structure.
Make reason 1 a felt benefit, reason 2 the value props, reason 3 the main objection.
Close with a CTA to the bundle offer.

test.method: A/B a numbered-reasons script against the current long-form script.

title: Write every hook to first stop the right viewer, then hold them
hypothesis: If a hook is written as a promise of relevance that first makes the right viewer stop and then keeps them past the first seconds, then it avoids winning attention from the wrong audience.

signal.check: Watch the first 3 seconds of a hook and ask who would actually stop for it. If the answer is 'anyone curious', not the target buyer, this idea is live.

expected_effect.size: most sources estimate about 80% of viewers drop at the hook

risk.note: Bait hooks such as memes or shock props win attention from the wrong people and lose the right ones.

steps: Write the hook so whoever appears or speaks in it is the target buyer.
Check the hook relates to what follows in the body.
Cut any bait element, such as a meme or shock prop, that has no link to the problem.

test.method: A/B a relevance-first hook against a bait-style hook on the same body.

title: Win the first frame against the next ad in the feed
hypothesis: If the first frame and first words give the target buyer a reason to stop within a fraction of a second, not just within the 3-second reporting window, then the hook beats the next ad in the feed instead of relying on a slow warm-up.

signal.check: Watch the first half-second of the hook. If nothing gives the target buyer a reason to stop yet, this idea is live.

expected_effect.size: sources disagree between about 0.5 seconds and a 3-second reporting window

risk.note: The 3-second hook rate is a reporting window, not a license to warm up slowly.

steps: Review the first frame and first spoken or written words in isolation.
Make sure they alone give the target buyer a reason to stop.
Move any slow visual or verbal warm-up out of the opening.

test.method: Compare hook rate between a fast-opening version and a slower warm-up version.

title: Avoid irrelevant bait hooks that teach delivery to find the wrong people
hypothesis: If a hook stays on-topic instead of using an irrelevant attention-grabber, then delivery does not learn to serve the ad to viewers who will never buy.

signal.check: Check whether a hook uses an off-topic attention grab, such as a meme with no product link, that still holds viewers who then bounce.

risk.note: The mechanism described (delivery learning from soft signals) is the presenters' belief, not confirmed platform documentation.

steps: Review each hook for whether its attention-grabbing element relates to the product's actual problem.
Replace an off-topic attention grab with an on-topic one.
Watch for unqualified clicks that bounce quickly as a sign the hook is training delivery on the wrong signal.

test.method: Compare CPA between an on-topic hook and an off-topic attention-grab hook.

title: Build every hook from three layers: audio, on-screen copy, and visual
hypothesis: If a hook is planned with a spoken line, on-screen text, and a visual, all three deliberately chosen, then fixing one weak layer can double its performance instead of the whole hook being wrongly blamed.

signal.check: Check whether the last hook brief specified only the visual, with no plan for the audio line or on-screen copy.

expected_effect.size: one anecdote reports adding an overlay line doubled hook rate

risk.note: A written hook with no visual plan can fail and be wrongly blamed on the words.

steps: For each hook, plan the audio line, the on-screen copy, and the visual separately.
Check all three point at the same problem and persona.
If a hook underperforms, test fixing one layer at a time before rewriting the whole hook.

test.method: Swap only the weakest layer on an underperforming hook and compare hook rate.

title: Grade every hook: clarity, relevance, novelty, then specificity and credibility
hypothesis: If every hook is scored on clarity, relevance, novelty, specificity, and credibility in that order, then weak hooks are caught before launch instead of after wasted spend.

signal.check: Check whether hooks are launched without any grading step against these 5 criteria.

risk.note: Low clarity and low relevance together fail a hook no matter how novel it is.

steps: Score each hook on clarity: does a stranger understand what it is within 3 seconds.
Score relevance: is the pain obvious to the target buyer.
Score novelty: has this been done many times before.
Score specificity and credibility: real numbers, names, or a trusted deliverer.
Drop any hook with low clarity and low relevance regardless of novelty.
For a hook meant to scale to very large spend, favor a genuinely novel angle over a standard type.

test.method: Compare hook rate of hooks scoring high on this grade against hooks that were not graded before launch.

title: Pick hooks from the proven type menu and avoid the two overused ones
hypothesis: If hooks are chosen from a menu of proven types such as contrarian truth, specific proof, or curiosity gap, and 'the number 1 mistake' or 'tactical promise' styles are avoided, then the batch skips types that have lost their edge or do not translate to ecommerce.

signal.check: Check whether the current hook uses the overused 'number 1 mistake' framing or a tactical-promise style with no product relevance.

risk.note: About 7 of the 9 listed types fit most ecommerce brands; not all will fit every category.

steps: Review the hook-type menu: problem agitation, contrarian truth, specific proof, curiosity gap, truth bomb, psychological confrontation, sensory, founder's letter, social proof.
Pick a type that fits the persona and stage.
Avoid 'the number 1 mistake' style and skip 'tactical promise' for ecommerce.
Name the hook type on the brief so it can be tracked.

test.method: Track hook rate by hook type over a quarter to see which types actually work for this account.

title: Open hooks with the problem, adding a persona label only when it widens relevance
hypothesis: If a hook agitates the viewer's exact problem and only adds a persona label when it carries the pain with it, then it avoids the weak, overrated demographic call-out that people skip.

signal.check: Check whether the current hook opens with a bare demographic label, such as 'agency owners, listen up', with no stated pain.

risk.note: Check any attribute-based call-out against the personal-attributes policy before launch.

steps: Open the hook with the viewer's exact problem, not a bare demographic label.
Add a persona call-out only when it carries the pain with it, for example naming who has the problem.
Run any attribute-based call-out past the compliance check.

test.method: A/B a problem-first hook against a demographic-label-only hook.

title: Never sell in the hook: no product name, image, or offer in the first line
hypothesis: If a cold hook contains no product name, no product on screen, and no offer, then it opens with an educational payoff instead of tipping the ad's hand and losing the viewer before the argument starts.
does_not_apply_when: a product-aware ad, per R54

signal.check: Check the first line and first frame of a cold ad's hook for the product name, image, or offer.

risk.note: None; this is a script rewrite step.

steps: Check the hook's first line and first frame for the product name, image, or offer.
Remove any of these from a cold ad's hook.
Replace the opening with an educational or problem-focused line.

test.method: A/B a hook with no product mention against one that names the product early.

title: Use curiosity in a hook only when it is tied to something the viewer wants answered
hypothesis: If a curiosity hook opens a gap the target buyer personally wants closed, instead of a generic mystery like a knife or a shocking prop, then it holds the right viewer instead of just anyone curious.

signal.check: Check whether the current curiosity hook would interest a random viewer as much as the target buyer.

risk.note: For statics, the destination page can absorb junk clicks from a broad curiosity hook; for video, this filter matters more.

steps: Write the curiosity gap so it names or implies the viewer's own problem or world.
Reject a gap that would interest a random viewer as much as the target buyer.
Where light and impulse categories allow, humor and in-group jokes can carry the curiosity.

test.method: A/B a qualified curiosity hook against a generic mystery-style hook.

title: Clear rights before using a famous face or trending term in a hook
hypothesis: If rights are cleared before a hook uses a famous face or trending term to borrow credibility, then the brand avoids the likeness and platform risk of using someone's identity without permission.

signal.check: Check whether the current hook references a public figure or trending term with no documented permission.

risk.note: Some presenters admit uncertainty about the legal risk here; do not treat 'brands seem to get away with it' as clearance.

prerequisites: A rights or permission process for names and likenesses
steps: Check whether the hook references a public figure, trending term, or third-party brand.
Confirm written permission or a licensing agreement exists before launch.
If permission cannot be confirmed, remove the reference.

test.method: None; this is a compliance gate, not a performance test.

title: Keep testing hooks post-Andromeda, but make each one truly different
hypothesis: If new hooks each change angle, offer, avatar, or format, then hook testing still finds new spend efficiency after Andromeda, even though slight wording variants get grouped and wasted.

signal.check: Check whether the team has stopped hook testing entirely, citing Andromeda grouping, without checking if past hooks were truly different.

expected_effect.size: one case: 50 new hooks on ads that had spent $50K to $100K added another $100K at the same efficiency

risk.note: The Andromeda grouping mechanism is described from memory by presenters, not confirmed platform documentation; re-verify periodically.

prerequisites: A proven body script to hang new hooks on
steps: Confirm the body script has already proven itself.
Write new hooks that each change at least one of angle, offer, avatar, or format.
Shoot the hooks as new footage rather than re-cutting old footage.
Launch and track whether the new hooks reach new audience or just re-serve the old one.

test.method: Track frequency and reach after launching truly different hooks on a fatigued winner.

title: Put more production time into hooks than into new body scripts once a body works
hypothesis: If more hooks are produced per proven body than new bodies per hook, then production time goes where the performance gap actually sits, since the hook usually explains more of the variance than the body.

signal.check: Check the last shoot's ratio of hooks produced to bodies produced. If bodies outnumber hooks once a script is proven, this idea is live.

expected_effect.size: 2 bodies by 15 hooks is claimed to beat 2 hooks by 5 bodies in the same production time

risk.note: If the body script itself is weak, one lucky body can distort what the team learns; fix the body first.

prerequisites: A body script that has already tested well
steps: Confirm the body script has already tested well.
Plan the next shoot to produce more hook variants than new body variants.
Build the body and CTA once, then test hooks against it.

test.method: Compare hit rate between a hook-heavy shoot plan and a body-heavy one.

title: Shoot many hooks per body but launch a budget-sized wave, holding the rest
hypothesis: If about 10 hooks are shot per body but only 2 to 4 are launched per wave, up to 8, sized to the daily budget, then each hook gets enough spend to exit learning instead of spreading budget too thin across too many hooks at once.

signal.check: Check whether the last launch put more hooks live per ad set than the daily budget could realistically fund to a read.

expected_effect.size: shoot about 10 hooks per body; launch 2 to 4 per body per wave, up to 8

risk.note: Never launch more hooks per body than the ad set's daily budget can take to a read.

prerequisites: Daily budget per pack and target CPA
steps: Shoot about 10 hooks per proven body.
Check the ad set's daily budget against target CPA to size the wave.
Launch 2 to 4 hooks per body in the first wave, up to 8 at most.
Hold the remaining hooks for the next wave or a future revival.

test.method: Compare per-hook delivery and read quality between a budget-sized wave and an oversized launch.

title: Vary hooks on four levers: angle, offer, avatar, and format
hypothesis: If hook variants change angle, offer, avatar, or format rather than just wording, then the variant set reaches viewers a wording-only change never would.

signal.check: Check the last hook variant set. If they all use the same speaker, offer, and visual with only different sentences, this idea is live.

risk.note: Wording changes alone bring in some viewers; visual changes are needed to reach the rest.

steps: List the 4 levers: angle (message or seasonal context), offer (bundle or sale, often in text), avatar (who delivers it), format (a static or motion-graphic intro).
For the next hook batch, vary at least one lever per variant.
Pair a lever change with volume, changing 1, 2, or all 4 across the set.

test.method: Compare reach and hook rate between a lever-varied set and a wording-only set.

title: Write only as many hooks as can bridge naturally into the body
hypothesis: If every hook is checked for a natural bridge into its body before production, then the shoot avoids wasting time on hooks that will feel disconnected once cut together.

signal.check: Read each planned hook against the body script and ask if the transition makes sense.

risk.note: A hook whose topic never appears in the body is a common, avoidable mistake.

prerequisites: A finished body script
steps: List candidate hooks alongside the body script's opening line.
Check each hook's topic appears somewhere in the body.
Cut hooks that do not bridge naturally, even if they are strong on their own.

test.method: Compare hold rate between hooks that pass the bridge check and ones that do not.

title: Do not spend test budget on CTA variants before hooks are tested
hypothesis: If test budget goes to hook variants before CTA variants, then it is spent where most viewers actually are, since average watch time means almost nobody reaches the CTA.

signal.check: Check whether the current test plan includes CTA variants before the hook has been tested.

risk.note: Test CTA variants only once volume targets demand it and hooks are already settled.

steps: Review the test plan for CTA-only variants.
Move CTA testing behind hook testing in priority.
Only test CTA variants once a volume target genuinely needs it.

test.method: None; this is a prioritization rule for the test plan, not itself a launchable test.

title: Read hook rate and hold rate against this account's own average, not an industry number
hypothesis: If hook rate and hold rate are compared to this account's own historical average, then a low reading is correctly diagnosed as a hook or bridge problem instead of being judged against an irrelevant industry figure.

signal.check: Check whether video reads are compared to an outside benchmark instead of the account's own trailing average.

expected_effect.size: unknown; neither metric correlates directly with conversions

risk.note: Hook and hold rate do not correlate with conversions on their own; use them to diagnose, not to declare a winner.

prerequisites: A tracked account-average hook rate and hold rate
steps: Compute the account's own trailing average hook rate and hold rate.
Compare each new ad's numbers to that average, not to an outside benchmark.
If hook rate is low, swap the hook and keep the body.
If hold rate is low, rewrite the bridge section.

test.method: Track the account average monthly and flag ads that fall meaningfully below it.

title: Validate hooks as trial reels before paid spend, where the page allows it
hypothesis: If hook and rough-cut ideas are posted as trial reels on the brand's page before paid spend, then a cheap read on reach and retention narrows the set before any ad dollars are spent.
does_not_apply_when: a page with no organic posting history to compare against

signal.check: Check whether the brand has an active page that could carry a trial reel, and whether hooks are currently tested only in paid.

expected_effect.size: post about 20 hook variants, keep the best, launch about 5 as ads

risk.note: If the page has no baseline posting history, skip this step and read in paid with a small pack instead.

prerequisites: An active brand or personal page with baseline posts
steps: Cut the CTA off the ad.
Post it as a trial reel on the page the ad will eventually run through.
Read reach against other posts and the retention graph for a weak hook, bridge, or body.
Feed the read into the next edit within 24 hours.
Post about 20 hook variants this way, keep the best, and launch about 5 as paid ads.

test.method: Compare paid hook rate on trial-reel-validated hooks against untested hooks.
test.read_point: After the paid pack's day 7 read

title: Move a strong mid-ad line to the start only if it stays clear
hypothesis: If a strong line found mid-ad is moved to the opening as a cheap test, then it may lift hook rate, but only if the moved line still makes clear what the ad is about.

signal.check: Check whether existing footage has a strong line buried mid-ad that could work as an opener.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one case lost relevance when moved without adjustment

risk.note: A moved line can lose relevance out of its original context; check clarity, not just novelty.

prerequisites: Existing footage with a strong mid-ad line
steps: Scan existing footage for a strong line that is currently buried mid-ad.
Cut a version that moves it to the opening.
Check the moved line still makes clear what the ad is about on its own.
Launch it as a cheap re-cut test.

test.method: Compare hook rate between the re-cut opener and the original ad.

title: Script founder ads as an argument, not a video of the founder talking
hypothesis: If a founder ad is scripted as an argument with a claim, proof, and mechanism, then it earns the authenticity the format promises instead of becoming raw, unscripted footage that reads as filler.

signal.check: Check whether the current founder ad is raw, unscripted footage with no argument structure.

risk.note: Most of the work is scripting and ideation, not filming; do not skip the script.

prerequisites: A founder willing to appear, or a chosen involvement level
steps: Write the founder's argument before filming: what is the claim, what is the proof, what is the mechanism.
Script the ad, do not rely on the founder chatting freely on camera.
Film only after the script is ready.

test.method: Compare conversion on a scripted argument-style founder ad against a raw, unscripted one.

title: Use the top founder structure: claim, proof, mechanism, proof, CTA with social proof
hypothesis: If founder ad bodies follow claim, immediate proof, mechanism tied to the founder story, proof of mechanism, then CTA plus social proof, then the structure matches what performed best in one agency's top founder ads by spend.

signal.check: Check whether the current founder script opens with a claim that is never proven.

expected_effect.size: unknown, from an unranked sample of one agency's top 15 founder ads

risk.note: The claim should usually be adversarial and double as the hook; keep it true.

steps: Open with an adversarial claim that doubles as the hook.
Prove the claim immediately.
Tie the unique mechanism to the founder's own story.
Prove the mechanism.
Close with a CTA plus social proof.

test.method: Compare conversion between the top-structure script and the account's current founder script format.

title: Build the founder story only from origin, mechanism, and adversarial angle
hypothesis: If the founder story is built from the 3 things only a founder can truly own, why the business started, why the product works, and what the category does wrong, then the story stays a genuine moat instead of relying on product experience anyone could claim.

signal.check: Check whether the founder story currently leans on product experience alone with no origin, mechanism, or adversarial angle.

risk.note: Run any adversarial or health-related claim past the compliance check.

prerequisites: True origin facts, lab or supplier proof
steps: Write the true origin: why the business started.
Write the mechanism: why the product works, said by the founder or a credentialed expert.
Write the adversarial angle: what the category does wrong, with proof.
Split these into static parts that stay consistent and renewable parts such as reviews and inbox items.

test.method: Compare conversion between a 3-element founder story and the current story format.

title: Tell the founder story through the viewer's problem, not the founder's biography
hypothesis: If a founder ad opens on a problem the viewer has lived and only then brings in the founder's solution, then the ad holds attention instead of losing viewers who do not care about the founder's life story.

signal.check: Check whether the founder script spends its first minute on the founder's biography before naming a problem the viewer shares.

risk.note: Founder-only stories with no viewer problem sometimes work, but the source says most of the time people don't care.

steps: Open on a problem the viewer has actually lived.
Agitate the problem before introducing the founder.
Open a curiosity gap that the founder's solution closes.
Walk through the mechanism, then close the gap.

test.method: A/B a viewer-first opening against a founder-biography-first opening on the same story.

title: Use only real, permissioned reviews and true founder stories, never scripted or altered
hypothesis: If every founder story detail, review, and email used in an ad is real and permissioned, then the brand avoids the disclosure and trust risk of a scripted review or an invented origin story presented as real.

signal.check: Check whether any review, email, or founder fact used in an ad is dramatized, invented, or lacks documented permission.

risk.note: A scripted review presented as real, or an altered origin story, is a compliance and brand-trust risk, not a creative choice.

prerequisites: Permission records for reviews and customer emails used
steps: List every review, email, and founder fact used in the ad.
Confirm each is real and, where it is a customer's own words, permissioned.
Reject any script that dramatizes, invents, or alters a story presented as real.
Also screen for any invented interview, whistleblower, or news-style format presented as real content.

test.method: None; this is a compliance gate, not a performance test.

title: Diversify founder ads by scene, format, and involvement level, in a batch pipeline
hypothesis: If founder ads vary by scene, format, and involvement level, and are batch-shot as a hook-by-body matrix on a monthly pipeline, then the founder's face stops being the account's strongest sameness signal.

signal.check: Check whether every founder ad uses the same scene, script role, and involvement level.

expected_effect.size: one case: a scene change alone added $40,000 of spend on the same script

risk.note: Change offer first as the easiest lever, then angle, then persona only with true stories.

prerequisites: A review and inbox feed for renewable material
steps: Reshoot a proven script in a new scene as a cheap first move.
Try a new format such as a tier list or store-aisle walk.
Move down the involvement spectrum: protagonist, voice-over B-roll, evidence, proxy, or absent.
Change the script role: protagonist, witness, interviewer, or reader.
Write 3 bodies with materially different stories times 10 hooks each for the monthly batch.
Pipe reviews and the support inbox into a database and pull relevant items weekly.

test.method: Track spend and frequency across founder ad variants over one quarter.

title: Run founder or creator partnership ads only through a page that already posts well
hypothesis: If a founder or creator partnership ad only runs through a handle that already posts often and relevantly, then it gets the claimed lift instead of underperforming a well-run company page.

signal.check: Check whether the founder or creator's personal page posts rarely or off-topic before defaulting to a partnership ad there.

expected_effect.size: expected lift 5% to 30%, not 10x, when the page qualifies

risk.note: One presenter says this arbitrage is fading; recheck against the brand's own results each quarter.

prerequisites: Access to set up a partnership ad, per current platform steps
steps: Check whether the founder or creator's own page posts often and relevantly.
If it does not, default to the company page instead.
If it does qualify, run the partnership ad and expect a 5% to 30% lift, not a 10x jump.
Recheck this quarterly against the brand's own side-by-side results.

test.method: A/B a partnership ad against the same ad run from the company page.

title: Use founder or in-house content as the human counter to AI-heavy creative
hypothesis: If the account keeps founder or in-house human content live alongside AI-assisted creative, then it counters the sameness of AI creative flooding many accounts, even though founder ads are optional, not mandatory.
does_not_apply_when: a founder who does not fit the persona or is unwilling to appear

signal.check: Check whether the account's live creative is almost entirely AI-generated with no real human presence.

risk.note: Founder-reliant ads still cap at the founder's own organic reach, so keep this as part of a portfolio, not the whole plan.

steps: Check what share of live creative is AI-generated versus real human content.
Add or keep at least one founder or in-house content pillar live.
Do not force founder ads on a founder who does not match the target persona.

test.method: Track account hit rate as the human-content share changes over a quarter.

title: Give every UGC brief a concept; UGC alone is not one
hypothesis: If a UGC brief always states its persona, angle, and offer instead of just requesting the format, then testing UGC teaches something instead of learning nothing from format alone.

signal.check: Check whether a current creator brief says only 'make a UGC video' with no persona, angle, or offer named.

risk.note: UGC still gives volume and authenticity AI cannot match; the fix is adding a concept, not dropping UGC.

steps: Write the persona, angle, and offer into every UGC brief.
Reject a brief that only names the format with no concept behind it.
Track results by concept, not just by 'UGC' as a category.

test.method: Compare hit rate on concept-led UGC briefs against format-only UGC briefs.

title: Brief creators in detail, allow 2 takes, and vet by the brief behind past work
hypothesis: If creators are vetted by the brief behind their best past work and cast for a native accent per market, then brief depth and casting match what actually produced their strongest results.

signal.check: Check whether creators are hired with no request for the brief behind their past work, or cast in a market that does not match their accent.

risk.note: A great result from a thin brief means broad strokes are fine for that creator; a detailed brief behind it means match that depth.

steps: Ask each creator for past work and the brief that produced it.
Match brief depth to what actually produced their best results.
Allow 2 takes: one held to script, one natural.
Cast native-accent creators for each market the ad will run in.

test.method: Compare conversion between creators vetted this way and creators hired with no vetting.

title: Source creative from in-house, UGC, and AI, and feed winners back across all three
hypothesis: If creative supply is split across in-house, UGC creators, and AI, and a winning idea from any pillar is rebuilt in the other two, then the account gets both control and volume instead of depending on one slow or one low-trust source.

signal.check: Check whether all current creative comes from a single source pillar with no cross-pollination when something wins.

expected_effect.size: starting heuristic near a third from each pillar, adjusted by what wins

risk.note: The one-third split is a starting heuristic, not a measured optimum; adjust it by what actually wins.

steps: Tag current creative supply by pillar: in-house, UGC, or AI.
Set a starting split near a third each, adjusted for the brand's speed and budget needs.
When an angle wins from one pillar, tell the creators, derive a static, and build in-house and AI versions of it.

test.method: Track hit rate by pillar and by whether winners were cross-built into the other pillars.

title: Build a standing creator roster and secure usage rights before paid use
hypothesis: If the brand runs an ongoing creator seeding program instead of one-off influencer deals, and secures rights before any paid use, then it builds a reusable content supply without a rights gap blocking a launch.
does_not_apply_when: a category or margin that cannot support product seeding at volume

signal.check: Check whether the brand gets only 1 video per creator sample with no ongoing roster, or moves organic content into paid without written rights.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one case reached about 5,800 videos from 100,000 invites in 60 days

risk.note: Moving organic or affiliate content into paid without rights and affiliate terms on file is a compliance gap.

prerequisites: Budget for product samples and a rights agreement template
steps: Invite creators broadly, approve, and ship samples.
Ask for 2 to 3 videos per sample and expect some creators who never post.
Run a lightweight creator community that learns what wins and reuse it for future launches.
Secure usage rights and affiliate terms in writing before any organic-to-paid move.

test.method: Track videos produced per sample shipped and the rights-on-file rate over one seeding round.

title: Split a fatigued testimonial into a new brand-side hook and the old customer body
hypothesis: If a fatigued testimonial ad gets a new 3-to-5-second brand-side opening while the customer testimonial body stays unchanged, then the ad gets a fresh hook without re-shooting the whole asset.

signal.check: Check whether a testimonial-based ad has fatigued but its body content is still strong.

risk.note: This is a single-source technique; treat it as one option among the fatigue-revival tactics.

prerequisites: A fatigued but otherwise strong testimonial ad
steps: Confirm the testimonial body is still strong and only the hook has fatigued.
Film a new 3-to-5-second brand-side opening that introduces the testimonial.
Cut it directly into the unchanged customer testimonial body.

test.method: Compare CPA of the new-hook version against the ad's pre-fatigue baseline.

title: Test removing the founder or influencer from an ad to open a new audience
hypothesis: If a founder- or influencer-led static is rebuilt without that person, showing a different persona instead, then the product can reach an audience segment the original talent's audience skews away from.
does_not_apply_when: a brand whose whole positioning depends on the founder or influencer being visible

signal.check: Check whether all current creative for the product features the same influencer or founder, with the audience skewing to their followers.

risk.note: Single-source technique; test on a small budget before assuming it opens a new segment.

steps: Identify the audience segment underrepresented in the current influencer-led creative.
Build a version of the static that shows a different persona instead of the founder or influencer.
Launch it targeted at the underrepresented segment.

test.method: Compare new-audience reach and CPA between the influencer version and the no-influencer version.

title: Make native short-form video that does not look like an ad
hypothesis: If TikTok or Reels creative uses raw storytelling and demos that open on the buyer's own habit or annoyance, then it reads as content, not an ad, and holds attention longer.

signal.check: Check whether current short-form creative looks like a polished studio ad rather than raw, relatable content.

risk.note: A visible studio rig on this format reads as an ad; keep the setting native.

steps: Open with the buyer's own habit or annoyance in the first line.
Keep the setting native, such as a car or home, not a studio.
Structure as raw storytelling or a demo, not a polished pitch.

test.method: Compare hold rate between a native-style cut and a studio-style cut of the same idea.

title: Pick a native TikTok or Reels format by the product's actual trait
hypothesis: If the native format is chosen to match the product's real trait, a visible first-use reaction, a flawed status quo, a slow-building result, or a common misconception, then the creative fits what the product can actually show instead of forcing a mismatched format.

signal.check: Check whether the current native video format was chosen at random rather than matched to a real product trait.

risk.note: For comparisons, show a generic old way failing honestly; never name or show a specific rival.

steps: Identify the product's real trait: strong first-use reaction, a rival's flaw, a slow result, a common misconception, a recurring annoyance, a surprising use, or a restricted desire.
Match it to the corresponding native format from the 7-format menu.
Write the relatable first line and structure hook, story or demo, then product and CTA at the back.
Plan a comment-reply follow-up video for strong questions the video draws.

test.method: Compare purchases per view across creator videos using a matched format versus a mismatched one.
test.read_point: After the video has enough views to compare

title: Judge creator video by purchases per view, not by views
hypothesis: If creator video success is judged by purchases per view instead of total views, then a low-view video with strong demonstration quality is not overlooked in favor of a high-view video that sells poorly.

signal.check: Check whether creator videos are currently ranked by view count with no purchase data attached.

expected_effect.size: one example: 34.5 million views produced fewer units than a lower-view video with better demonstration

risk.note: Requires views, orders, and revenue tracked per creator video.
